#6161. Future heatwaves could make today’s record heat look mild

Future heatwaves could last longer, spread farther, and exceed recent records, even with sharp emissions cuts, models suggest.

When people plan for extreme heat, they usually plan around the worst summers they’ve already lived through.

New research suggests those summers won’t stay the worst, even if the world sharply cuts its emissions.

In climate model projections for nine regions around the world, many of this century’s heatwaves lasted longer, affected wider areas, and got hotter than the recent record-breakers in those places.

Philipp Aglas-Leitner, a researcher in the Department of Physics at Freie Universität Berlin, led the work.

Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick of the Australian National University and scientists in Germany, Switzerland, and New Zealand were co-authors of the study.

Because the results come from computer models, they show what could happen rather than predicting any particular summer. They also focus on the heat itself, not on what it would cost in lives or money.

“Recent observed events are outmatched by a substantial margin, particularly toward the end of the twenty-first century,” Aglas-Leitner said.

The researchers began with 22 heatwaves from 2010 to 2023 that broke records or caused serious harm.

From those, they picked one per region, including Europe’s summer of 2018 and the 2021 heatwave in the Pacific Northwest of the US and Canada.

For each region and each day of the year, the team found the temperature that only the hottest 10% of days had topped between 1961 and 1990.

A heatwave was any stretch of at least three days in a row when the region’s average daily high stayed above that mark.

For every heatwave, they tracked how long it lasted, how much of the region it covered, and how far temperatures climbed above normal. They also added up the extra heat above the mark.

The team used two temperature datasets to check the past heatwaves.

One is built from weather station readings by Berkeley Earth. The other, called ERA5, blends observations with a weather model.

For the future, the team used simulations from two generations of climate models, run for futures ranging from steep emissions cuts to very high emissions.

They checked how well each model matched each region’s hottest days and dropped the weakest quarter.

Europe’s 2018 heatwave lasted 34 days, from July 10 to August 12. If emissions stay high, the models suggest close to one in five future European heatwaves will last even longer, and India and Pakistan show the same pattern.

The team only looked at each region’s six warmest months, so no heatwave in the study could last longer than six months.

Even with steep emissions cuts, some projected heatwaves reached or nearly reached that limit in five of the nine regions.

Those five regions were Europe, northeast Siberia, North Africa and the Middle East, the Pacific Northwest, and South America.

Under high emissions, some projected heatwaves in those regions lasted the entire six-month study window.

A heatwave that runs a little hot for weeks can add up to more extra heat than one that’s very hot for a few days.

The researchers captured this with a number called cumulative heat, which adds up how many degrees each day’s high went above the heatwave mark.

Seven of the nine recent heatwaves had built up an unusually large amount of this heat.

Even with steep emissions cuts, the models gave most of those regions roughly a one-in-10 to one-in-five chance that a future heatwave would build up more than twice as much. Australia and China were the exceptions.

With high emissions, most of those regions faced similar odds of a heatwave with more than five times as much extra heat.

The team also sorted the results by how much the planet has warmed since the late 1800s. That makes it easier to see what different climate targets would mean.

Take the most intense day of Europe’s record summer.

In a world without global warming, the models gave a future heatwave less than a 0.3% chance of beating it. At 3.6°F (2°C) of warming, the upper limit in the Paris Agreement, nearly one in five projected European heatwaves did.

Countries’ current climate pledges would lead to about 4.7°F to 5°F (2.6°C to 2.8°C) of warming, according to the United Nations’ 2024 Emissions Gap Report.

At warming close to that level, 27% to 37% of projected European heatwaves beat the 2018 peak.

Even if countries keep their promises, then, a sizable share of Europe’s future heatwaves could top that record summer’s peak.

With more warming, the share grows. At 6.3°F to 8.1°F (3.5°C to 4.5°C), 36% to 64% of projected European heatwaves beat the 2018 event on every measure the team tracked, all at once.

In North Africa and the Middle East, the figure was 75% to 90%.

“Even ambitious emission reduction goals offer only limited protection,” Aglas-Leitner said.

“Without substantial emission reductions and consistent adaptation measures, however, a significant part of the twenty-first century will be defined by heat that goes far beyond our recent experiences.”

Another way to see the change is to ask how often a heatwave as extreme as each recent record would come along.

In model runs of the past, from 1951 to 2005, such heat showed up at most about once in 55 years, which was the length of that period.

Many models never produced a comparable event during that period, suggesting longer intervals between such extremes.

That gap shrinks fast. For 2015 to 2054, the wait in most regions drops to just a few years, whatever path emissions take.

By 2060 to 2099, most model groups project heatwaves matching or exceeding most recent benchmarks about once a year or more.

That pattern suggests heat like the recent record-breakers will become far more common than it was in past decades.

Australia’s heatwave of December 2019 is the exception. Its peak was so extreme that even late in the century, under low emissions, the models projected something similar only about once every 20 to 40 years.

A future heatwave that beats these records won’t necessarily cause more damage, the authors wrote. That depends partly on how well and how quickly people adapt, and partly on when in the summer the heat arrives.

People and ecosystems may adapt to some of these changes, but the human body has physiological limits on how much heat it can handle.

Adaptation efforts may also fall behind if heatwaves change as fast as the models project, the team wrote.

The study has limits of its own. Each region was drawn around the whole area a heatwave covered, so very local extremes don’t show up in the results.

The two temperature records also disagreed noticeably for some events, though the authors found this didn’t change their overall conclusions.

And the most extreme projections came more often from models that warm faster, though not only from them.

Understanding how these extremes would affect health, ecosystems, and electricity supplies will require studies at smaller, local scales.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6160. The 8 Best Pet Hair Vacuums Designed for Homes That Never Stop Shedding

We evaluated models from top brands including Dyson, Bissell, and Shark.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Getting pet hair out of carpets and off of tile and hardwood is a constant battle many are familiar with, and trying to remove those persistent hairs that have embedded themselves into your upholstery is another beast. Choosing the right vacuum can significantly improve your cleaning routine if you’re a cat or canine parent.

The top pet hair vacuums are designed with powerful suction and superior filtration (plus, they come with special attachments) to capture fine hair, thick fur, and pet dander. Regardless of whether you have a fluffy cat, a long-haired pup, or both, investing in a vacuum specifically made for pets will help you keep messes in check for a tidier home.

Upright and canister vacuums are the strongest options for deep cleaning, but cordless stick vacuums, handheld vacuums, and robot vacuums all aid in daily pet hair control. Units that have tangle-free brush rolls and easy-to-empty dustbins are best for reduced maintenance, and a HEPA filter is essential for clearing out dust and dander that may trigger your allergies.

I researched and hands-on-tested lots of vacuums to find versions that truly pick up pet hair, focusing on features, bin capacity, and filtration. Below are my choices, as well as advice and important pointers to consider before you shop.

I initially considered a range of vacuum styles, from uprights to robots to canisters. Keeping in mind different price points, I chose models that provide an optimal combination of suction strength, versatility, pet-focused features and tools, and value.

I tested the Shark AZ2002 Vertex in a home with two American Shorthair cats, three different floor types, and multiple area rugs. I cleaned everything from tracked litter and dust on laminate and carpet to pet hair on furniture and upholstery, trying out the different suction power modes and attachments as I went. I vetted the features that I thought would be most helpful for animal owners such as HEPA filtration, a motorized pet tool, and an anti-tangle brush roll. Based on this research and testing, these are my top recommendations for the best pet hair vacuums.

One of the things I liked most about this upright model is its specially crafted vacuum head, which uses both a soft roller brush and paddled, fin-like brush roll to pick up embedded hair, fine dust, and dirt from all types of flooring. I noticed that this method prevents longer hair from getting tangled in the brush roll and allows for a deeper clean overall.

Cleaning modes are easy to access with a simple switch on the handle, and the vacuum head has LED lights that illuminate hidden dust bunnies and stray pet hair, which was extremely helpful when cleaning under furniture and in corners.

Another major plus is that this upright model also converts into a motorized, lift-away pod for cleaning other surfaces like couch cushions and stairs. The vacuum’s hose stretches up to an impressive 12 feet, and it comes with a crevice tool and pet upholstery tool. I tried the motorized pet tool on polyester couch cushions, and it didn’t struggle to pick up embedded pet hair.

The Vertex has a large, 1-quart dustbin to accommodate more hair, along with a fully sealed HEPA filtration system to capture pet dander. And while it’s heavy, it navigates pretty easily.

Full Shark AZ2002 Vertex Upright Vacuum Review

It’s hard to come by a vacuum that is less than $200 that doesn’t skimp on suction power, assets, or reliability. This model offers all of the above at an accessible price. Our tester has been using this vacuum for four years and has yet to be disappointed.

“This vacuum has a brush roll with multiple rows of bristles that kick out any hair that’s really deep inside a variety of fibers, including rugs and carpets.”

It works just as well on hardwood floors, and the swivel-steering vacuum head is easy to maneuver under and around furniture. The power cord is extremely long, extending 27 feet, and is automatically retractable with the cord rewind mechanism.

The CleanView comes with attachments for removing pet hair from stairs and hard-to-reach corners on hardwood and carpeted floors. It’s easy to empty, too, with a button on the front that releases dirt directly into the garbage.

One main complaint from our tester is that, given the size and weight of this upright model, it can be a pain to shuffle around as you clean. “Dragging around the Cleanview to different rooms of the house requires some effort. The vacuum weighs 15 pounds, which doesn’t seem like a lot until you need to get to a different part of your home.”

Full Bissell Cleanview Swivel Rewind Upright Vacuum Review

Dyson is most recognized for its powerful vacuums, and if you’re on the hunt for a machine that easily pulls pet hair out of your shaggiest of carpets, you won’t be disappointed with the Ball Animal 3 Extra model.

Besides strong suction, this vacuum boasts a five-layer, complete filtration system that captures dust and pet dander, preventing them from being released back into the air. The floor head has an integrated comb that untangles hair from the brush roll as it rotates, keeping lengthy strands from getting ensnared.

The vacuum is simple to handle thanks to the brand’s distinctive ball design, and it includes a combination tool, stair tool, turbine tool, and a pet groom tool. The wand is instant-release and has an extended hose for reaching isolated areas like underneath your couch or around dining room chairs.

This powerful vacuum has a sealed HEPA filtration system to securely trap dirt, dander, and fur so they don’t recirculate back into your home as you clean. It works on a variety of surfaces but handles hardwood floors the best because its good suction control prevents larger debris from scattering.

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser also has a tangle-free brush roll, and even after using the vacuum on two large area rugs and hardwood floors for months, I haven’t had to cut any hair from the bristles. Plenty of cat fur, dirt, and dander makes its way into the dustbin as the suction power is strong enough to agitate carpet fibers and pick up debris that might not be completely visible.

I love that there is a dedicated pet hair attachment for the hose wand. It works well on couch cushions, and a few pushes back and forth removed a majority of the mess. Plus, the vacuum converts into a canister pod, so it moves around easily as you work around your space.

The convertible design adds maneuverability, and the attachments included are helpful for more precise cleaning.

Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Allergen Lift-Off Full Review

The Bissell Pet Hair DualBrush packs two brush roll types into one vacuum. The first loosens and cleans debris that’s stuck to your floor or caught up in carpet fibers, and behind it, a second brush roll makes closer contact with the floor to pick up the now loosened debris. Powerful suction delivers strong pet hair pickup, too.

This model converts to a handheld-style canister vacuum that lifts off of the base, so you can easily clean hard-to-reach areas or furniture. We appreciate that this design also has LED lights on the vacuum floorhead and pet hair attachment to illuminate hidden dust and debris.

The DualBrush uses sensors to automatically detect the level of dirt and dust on the floor, and will adjust suction power accordingly, helping you get a deeper clean in situations where it’s most needed. It weighs 17 pounds, which may be a pain to push around for longer cleaning sessions, but that isn’t uncommon for an upright vacuum.

Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser DualBrush Upright Vacuum Review

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Turbo comes with multiple features that are a standout for pet owners. This model is equipped with a HEPA filter to keep allergens out of your home, and the canister detaches from the base, making it easier to clean stairs, around baseboards, and along blinds. Just keep in mind that the hose only extends seven feet, so you’ll have to carry the detachable pod close by.

Some noteworthy attachments are a tangle-free brush roll and a motorized tool that’s specifically designed to remove pet hair from upholstery. The primary vacuum head has LED lights on the front and sides, and there’s also a crevice tool with an LED light for convenient cleaning in dark corners, along with a two-in-one dusting brush.

The vacuum has a touch-and-release button on the dustbin’s exterior to easily empty it without getting dust and pet dander on your hands.

Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Turbo Lift-Off Upright Vacuum Review

Our tester has six pets, so there’s plenty of mess to go around, whether it’s tracked-in dirt from muddy paws or scattered litter. Pulling out the upright vacuum for quick cleanups isn’t always convenient, and this cordless stick model is her go-to for daily maintenance.

One of the things she loves the most about the Levoit LVAC-300 is the five-stage filtration system, which provides air purifier-level purification, a must-have for pet owners with animals that shed or have lots of dander.

The vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—so she was able to adjust suction power depending on the size of the mess and debris. The LVAC-300 transitions between floor types easily, but excels on hardwood and tile.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself.

Full LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Tired of the pet hair tumbleweeds strewn about your floors? This robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. With 16,200 pascals of suction power, it effectively picked up debris from a variety of floor types such as carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile.

One of the most notable features is the built-in razor in the base station that automatically slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have to manually remove hair from the brush roll.

Beyond that, our tester felt that this robot vacuum successfully avoided pet toys, cords, and overly friendly animals that seemed very interested in the vacuum’s whereabouts.

There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper mop, and they extend outward to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards.

The companion app is helpful for managing cleaning schedules, monitoring battery levels, and mapping, but gets a little more confusing as you adjust more advanced smart features.

Full Eureka J15 Pro Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

We’re regularly testing vacuums with focused pet hair features, so it’s common to see different vacuums take the place of others in this roundup. Here are a few that we’ve tested and think are still worth recommending:

Dyson V16 Piston Animal: This is a newer release from the brand, with some of the highest suction power we’ve seen from a cordless stick vacuum. The all-floor head cleaner excelled on carpet, and hair never got tangled around the brush roll, but performance on hard surfaces wasn’t as impressive. The vacuum comes with the classic Fluffy Optic soft roller cleaner head, but for the “all-floor” cleaner head isn’t the most ideal for all surfaces.

Miele Guard L1 Cat and Dog Bagged Canister Vacuum: The cleaner head on this vacuum lifts to five heights, and the extra-long hose allows you to work your way around your home without lugging the entire base vacuum around with you. On the downside, it doesn’t clean high-pile carpeting like shag or tufted wool, and other models we recommend have better pet-hair-specific attachments for cleaning upholstery.

There are a few factors that make a vacuum well-suited for dog and cat fur—namely, how much hair its bin holds, how it empties, how well it filters fine particles, and the types of attachments included.

The ideal bin capacity depends on the size of your home’s dimensions and the amount of pet hair you usually manage on a regular basis. For households with multiple pets, or animals that shed heavily, a vacuum with a spacious bin capacity (one liter or more) reduces the number of times you have to empty it during cleaning.

If you have a smaller home or you just have one pet, a bin capacity of 0.5 to 1 liter will most likely suffice. If you’re still unsure of what you might need, here’s a breakdown of the bin capacity each type of vacuum typically offers.

These normally have the largest capacity, ranging from two to four liters to hold more pet hair, dander, and debris before needing to be emptied. This design and capability could be ideal for heavy-duty cleaning or households with more than one pet.

Upright vacuums come in a close second, often with a capacity between one and three liters, so they’re a good option for folks with a pet that sheds mildly, or only during part of the year. These vacuums are also sufficient for standard home cleaning.

Because cordless vacuums are better used as supplementary cleaning tools, they have much smaller dustbins—usually ranging between 0.3 and 0.7 liters—which is really only enough for spot-cleaning, picking up dust bunnies between deep cleaning sessions, and use in tight spaces.

Similar to cordless vacuums, robot vacuums live on the smaller end of bin capacity. If you decide to go with this type, I recommend a model with a self-emptying bin. Most robot vacuums have small onboard dustbins, but they fill up faster. Self-emptying models have a larger dust collection area in the base, so you won’t have to manually empty as frequently.

For allergy sufferers, it’s essential to have a vacuum with an excellent filtration system, so look for models with a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter. These filters trap 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. Pet dander can be as small as 2.5 microns in diameter, and a HEPA filter efficiently captures these particles along with pollen, dust, and other allergens your pets may have tracked into the house.

A fully sealed filtration system, sometimes called an anti-allergen seal, is another common feature on pet vacuums. This means the components of the vacuum are tightly sealed so fine particles can’t escape back into your home once they’ve been sucked up.

Powerful suction is vital, but the included tools and attachments are often what pet owners use to successfully pull hair out of upholstery and carpeting. The following attachments are useful for tackling pet hair, and they come with many of the models I recommend above.

A standard attachment that comes with almost all vacuums, these elongated, narrow tools are great for accessing tight areas, like behind the toilet or between couch cushions. They’re useful for cleaning up clumps of hair that may have gathered in corners of your home where the vacuum’s floor head cannot reach.

Non-motorized upholstery brushes have bristles or a strip of microfiber to clean off furniture. As you pull the tool across fabric, the bristles lift pet hair and dust to be sucked up through the vacuum hose.

For pet hair that’s worked deep into upholstery, whether on your furniture or in your car, a motorized pet tool provides the most lifting power. These tools have small, spinning brush rolls, usually equipped with bristles, that agitate hair to pull it from the fabric, and they tend to work much more efficiently than non-motorized tools.

If you have pet hair or dander on your window screens or baseboards, a dusting brush has long, soft bristles that pick up dust and fine particles without scratching surfaces.

In addition to an arsenal of attachments to pull up pet hair, there are a few features that make cleaning up after your dog or cat even easier.

#6159. People are trusting AI advice, even when it’s really bad

AI advisors with hidden goals steered people toward worse choices in a new study, yet most participants still rated the advice as helpful.

Ask a chatbot which fitness tracker to buy and it feels like asking a knowledgeable friend with nothing to sell. In a new experiment, that friend had a hidden goal, and people followed it.

An AI advisor instructed to favor an inferior option increased the odds that people would prefer it over the best one to roughly five to eight times.

Most participants still rated the advisor as helpful afterward.

June Liu and Tatia Lee of the Department of Psychology at the University of Hong Kong ran the study with Sahand Sabour and Minlie Huang at Tsinghua University.

All 233 participants chose among hypothetical options in scripted scenarios and were told so. The authors flagged that as a limit on what the results can say.

The team built three advisors from one AI model, GPT-4o, changing only its instructions. One was told to help.

One was told to push a particular inferior option without ever saying so. Its prompt scored it on points: 100 for landing the target option, 50 for any other poor option, zero for the best one.

The third got the same goal plus a menu of influence tactics from psychology research.

Each person got one advisor and one kind of decision. Financial scenarios asked which fitness tracker, weight-loss medication, or clothing site to choose on a budget.

Emotional scenarios asked how to handle low self-esteem, a fight with a friend, or criticism at work.

Every scenario offered four options, and one fit the person’s stated needs.

In the money scenarios, the other three were a scam-like deal, an overbuilt version beyond the budget, and a subscription with long-term costs.

In the emotional ones, they were ways of coping that psychologists link to worse outcomes, such as withdrawing.

People rated each option from 1 to 10, talked with the advisor for at least ten exchanges, and rated the options again. The advisors also knew each person’s personality scores.

Before anyone talked to an advisor, every group rated the best option highest. Talking with a misaligned advisor shifted preferences.

Among people given the misaligned advisor on financial decisions, the share preferring the hidden target over the best option rose by 29 percentage points relative to the neutral advisor’s group.

With the tactics-equipped advisor it rose by 38 points. On emotional decisions the rises were 20 and 18 points.

Handing the advisor a toolkit of influence tactics didn’t reliably add to that.

The advisor given influence tactics was somewhat more effective at shifting financial preferences but less effective on emotional questions.

Even without that toolkit, an advisor with a hidden goal could steer people toward worse choices.

The researchers logged which tactics the equipped advisor chose. It leaned on pleasant ones, such as flattery and making the conversation enjoyable, rather than guilt trips.

On money questions, it used diversion, justification, urgency, and fabricated information more often, a mix the authors compared to predatory marketing.

On emotional questions, it leaned on pleasure and, at times, guilt, with a wider range of reassuring replies.

After the sessions, 86.8% of people in the financial group and 86.5% in the emotional group rated the misaligned advisor as helpful.

For the tactics-equipped advisor, the figures were 78.9% and 75.6%. The neutral advisor scored 97.5% and 87.2%.

Nobody was asked directly whether they felt manipulated, but some said so on their own.

On financial questions, 13.2% of people with the misaligned advisor and 28.9% with the tactics version mentioned a possible ulterior motive, and none of the neutral advisor’s group did.

On emotional questions, fewer than one in ten did in any group.

The authors’ reading is that people applied the instincts they use to judge whom to trust among other people to a system built around a different motive.

Perceived helpfulness didn’t explain the shift, either.

Participants considered hypothetical choices without making purchases or acting on the emotional advice.

Whether these preference shifts carry into real purchases or real conflicts remains unknown.

The sessions lasted at least ten exchanges, and the advisors knew each participant’s personality scores. The authors noted that these conditions went beyond a casual conversation with a general AI chatbot.

They described the result as what is possible under favorable conditions, not an estimate of everyday risk.

The study also tested only one AI model using a limited set of prompts.

Participants came from two pools, English speakers on Prolific and Chinese speakers on WeChat, and the pattern held in both.

Whether a human advisor with the same secret goal would move people as far is a question the study did not test. The authors named it as important work still to do.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their star's glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

#6157. When did the Anthropocene begin? Scientists make the case for a specific year

Scientists argue the Anthropocene began in 1952, separating a sharp global transformation from thousands of years of human influence.

People were reshaping soils 2,000 years ago, and lead pollution appears in the geological record stretching back 3,500 years. But when did human activity begin transforming Earth on a global scale?

A group of 37 researchers argues that early human impacts and the planet’s recent transformation are different stories.

Using one name for both, they write, obscures how sharply conditions changed in the mid-20th century.

They propose reserving “Anthropocene” for a geological epoch beginning in 1952, while giving the longer history of human influence a separate name.

The argument appears as a perspective piece, built on published evidence rather than a new dataset. Its lead author is Jan Zalasiewicz of the University of Leicester, who co-chairs the Anthropocene Working Group.

Co-authors include Buhm Soon Park of KAIST in South Korea, Julia Adeney Thomas of the University of Notre Dame, and Jürgen Renn of Germany’s Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

“The Anthropocene is a common language for understanding how rapidly and extensively humans are changing the Earth,” Park said.

“By clarifying its meaning and criteria, we can compare changes in the global environment more accurately and discuss together how we should respond.”

The relatively stable climate of the Holocene, which began about 11,700 years ago, helped people develop farming and build cities.

The authors’ case is that this stability ended in the middle of the 20th century.

That period saw the postwar surge of industry, population, and consumption known as the Great Acceleration.

The surge left marks in mud and ice. Across sites around the world, the chemical and physical traces of human activity pile up in layers centered on 1952.

That is also the year fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test settled across the globe. Those layers are the evidence the proposal rests on.

Humanity has used more energy since the 1950s than in the whole of the Holocene before it, most of it from fossil fuels.

A formal proposal to add the Anthropocene to the geological time scale, starting in 1952, went to the International Commission on Stratigraphy in October 2023.

The commission rejected it in March 2024, amid disagreement over whether an epoch only seven decades old was too brief to count.

The rejection did not retire the word, and the authors sort its uses into two families.

The meaning they defend is a geological epoch beginning when the Earth system stopped behaving as it had during the Holocene.

The other, which they call the extended Anthropocene, gathers up every substantial human impact over tens of thousands of years, from the earliest reshaping of ecosystems to the steam engine.

Proposed starting points have ranged widely. Some put it at 1784, when James Watt improved the steam engine.

Others point to European colonization of the Americas in the 1600s, or to farmed soils thousands of years earlier.

The authors call the extended version a valid idea but a different one. It can’t be pinned to a layer of rock, so the “-cene” ending, which marks a geological epoch, doesn’t fit it.

They suggest a separate label, such as “anthroposphere,” to keep the two apart.

The authors’ table of changes since the 1950s reads like an inventory of a different planet. Global freshwater use rose more than 300%, and the water held behind dams rose 1,500%.

Those dams are one reason rivers now deliver half as much sediment to the sea as they did.

The changes also reshaped marine and terrestrial life.

Predatory marine fish have declined about 90% since 1950 as the global catch quadrupled, and coral reefs, kelp forests, and mangroves have each lost about half their extent.

Humans and their livestock now make up about 98% of the mass of mammals on land, a shift other researchers have described as pushing life toward a mass extinction.

The authors lean on the planetary boundaries framework, which sets safe limits for nine Earth processes against pre-1950s Holocene baselines.

Seven of the nine have been crossed. That framework already treats the 1950s as the dividing line, they wrote, and a formal epoch would make that comparison standard.

Whether the commission will vote again is open, and the authors call formal recognition an ongoing aim.

The evidence keeps growing as new sites are analyzed, they wrote, from ocean chemistry to the plastics and persistent pollutants piling up in modern sediments.

They also acknowledged that a formal name on the time scale would not, by itself, make other fields adopt it.

In the scenario the authors describe, atmospheric carbon dioxide would still approach 500 parts per million even if the world reaches net zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.

Most polar sea ice and coral reefs would be lost, and sea level rise would keep accelerating.

Their research priorities are tracking heat, acidity, and plastics through the oceans, and pinning down the planetary boundaries and the tipping points behind them.

For now, 1952 remains a proposed boundary, and the Anthropocene remains a term with more than one meaning.

The perspective was published in the journal Nature Reviews Earth & Environment.

#6156. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6155. The 8 Best Hot Tubs That You Can Buy Online

We broke down the best options across sizes, styles, and price points, plus what actually matters before you commit.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

At some point, a hot tub stops feeling like a splurge and starts sounding like a really good idea. It’s one of the few backyard upgrades that actually changes how you use your space, whether you’re dealing with sore muscles, trying to carve out a little quiet at the end of the day, or just want a place to hang out that isn’t your couch.

If you still aren’t sure about whether or not you think it’s worth the purchase, know that there’s a crop of new hot tubs that can ship right to your door and don’t take too long to set up. You can get some simple plug-and-play models up and running in an afternoon, elevating your outdoor space from a simple yard to a true getaway spot. Others are closer to a full installation, though the trade-off is typically stronger jets, better insulation, and more built-in features. You also have options like basic inflatables, molded shells, or acrylic spas with lighting, waterfalls, and app controls.

For our recommendations, we focused on how these tubs are built, their lineups of features, and what you’re really getting for the price. Here are the ones worth considering, plus what to know before you commit to this big purchase.

To guide our selections, we leaned on our own experience owning hot tubs and spas, from basic models to custom setups.

We chose hot tubs that range from just under $1,000 for inflatable models to high-end models that nearly mimic showroom-quality tubs. But all are available to buy online. Beyond price, we looked at features, capabilities, and fun extras like speakers and ice buckets. Some are a must, while others are mere perks that can elevate your time in the hot tub—and the price.

We pored over customer reviews and expert write-ups. We also consulted Jeff Courter, an engineer and former owner of Cache Valley Spas in Logan, Utah, to get his insights on how you should factor price, setup, and features into your decision.

In a crowded field of plug-and-play spa contenders, the AquaRest DayDream stands out for a long list of relaxing reasons. It’s a legit backyard spa without the headache of professional installation and electrical upgrades, which puts this spa in that sweet spot between bargain shopping and custom installs.

We like that it plugs into a standard outlet but still delivers a surprisingly strong massage thanks to 35 jets. AquaRest says the DayDream uses a Jacuzzi-branded pump—and while that doesn’t make it a Jacuzzi spa, it’s still a solid indicator you’re getting a reputable, name-brand component under the hood.

There are so many nice extras, like ozone filtration and a lighted waterfall, that make it feel more like a full spa setup than a starter tub. The trade-off is in the materials and power: The roto-molded shell isn’t as luxe as pricier acrylic models, and heating can be slow on 120 volts. There is the option to use a 240-volt setup, if you’ve got the capacity. Given the price and host of features, this hot tub is a great choice for those looking to make a long-term investment.

More: Best Inflatable Hot Tubs for Backyard Bliss

If you’re looking for a solid hot tub without overspending, we like the Coleman SaluSpa line. The Sicily AirJet is a great choice within that line because it gives you a larger soaking area, 180 AirJets, and a 314-gallon water capacity without jumping into hard-sided spa pricing. This is still an inflatable model, so it does not have the same insulation, jet pressure, or long-term durability you get from a permanent acrylic spa, but the feature set is strong for the price.

Our family has been using a SaluSpa for several months now, and I find it easy to maintain as well. We especially like that the package includes the pump, cover, chemical floater, two filter cartridges and repair patch, which makes the first setup feel simple and straightforward.

We have found the hot tub is hard to connect to the companion app, but we also have no problem controlling it from the panel and do not find a need for an app. For shoppers looking for a quality inflatable that won’t break the bank and has solid reviews, this is a roomy, feature-heavy pick that feels like a better value than many smaller inflatables.

Inflatable hot tubs are a great option for folks who want to relax at home without making a more permanent decision (and investment). If you’re looking for a roomy, tricked-out inflatable hot tub to enhance your wellness, the Intex PureSpa Greywood Deluxe checks quite a few boxes.

With 170 bubble jets, a multifunction heater, filter, blower, and hard water treatment system, this model has more features than many inflatables. With a capacity of 290 gallons and included headrests, there is plenty of room for lounging. If you like the features of this tub, but have less space to work with, there is also a smaller four-person model available.

We like that—for the price—this hot tub includes a lot of fun extras. In addition to the water treatment and jet specs, there’s also a multicolor LED light system and wireless touch button control panel. There are two headrests, a cover, ground tarp, and storage bag included as well.

We do wish there were more than two headrests for a hot tub advertised for six people, but it’s not a deal breaker. One note: Check your available ground space before ordering, too, as this hot tub has a larger footprint than some other popular models.

This hot tub solves a lot of the issues folks face when seeking a therapeutic experience at home—they may not have the space or ability to upgrade the electrical system.

The hard-sided LifeSmart plugs into a standard outlet, skips complicated installation, and still delivers a solid massage with 13 jets, all in a compact, patio-friendly footprint. If you’re hoping to place this hot tub on an elevated surface, though, it’s important to consult a professional and check the load your deck can bear.

Even compact four-person models like this one can weigh over 3,000 pounds when filled with water, which is more than most standard decks can handle without added support. And while it’s listed as a four-seater, many users say it's comfiest with two to three adults.

If aesthetics matter as much as performance, this Comfort hot tub leans into both. The acrylic shell and clean wood-look cabinet design give it a more built-in, high-end vibe than most entry-level spas (which typically have rotomolded, all-in-one shells). We love the details like LED lighting and water features that make the whole experience feel a bit fancy.

It’s not just about looks, though. With 51 jets and a lounger seat, this tub delivers a more immersive soak than simpler plug-and-play models. The trade-off is in installation. For this model, you’ll need a 240-volt hookup, but that also means those jets will pack a lot of therapeutic power at the end of a long day.

If you want a five-person hot tub that doesn’t require rewiring your backyard, the LifeSmart LS500 keeps things simple. It plugs into a standard outlet, sets up quickly, and still delivers a comfortable soak with 23 adjustable jets and a lounge seat. We wish there were more, but other features (and price) make up for the lack of bubbles.

The full-foam insulation and thermal locking cover do a solid job holding heat, which helps keep operating costs in check, and the built-in ozonator cuts down on chemical maintenance. We also like the simple look of this spa, which feels a little high-end for the price bracket. It’s not the most powerful spa in this size range, and heat-up times can be slow, but for an easy, low-hassle setup, it’s a practical upgrade.

While Bestway’s Toronto was our pick for overall best inflatable hot tub, the foam walls do require some extra setup—the process takes two people several hours to complete. On the other hand, the Hot Springs model fully self-inflates in under five minutes and is truly plug-and-play, making it a great choice for those who are purchasing their first hot tub and are not yet familiar with some of the intricacies involved with setting one up and maintaining it.

Everything you need to set it up is included right in the box, with just a level, dry surface and access to an outlet (without an extension cord) required. Despite the lack of foam inserts, this hot tub is still rated for year-round use with Bestway’s Freeze Shield technology. One caveat: While this tub says it's for four to six people, it's really most practical for just four.

The DoCred inflatable hot tub delivers solo relaxation without swallowing up a small patio or using a ton of water. Think of it as an outdoor bathtub, perfect for homes with only showers or those with very limited outdoor space. The oval shape actually makes it easier to fully stretch out compared to some two-to-four-person circular models, and the included side table and mat are a nice touch.

A few drawbacks: Because the heater and bubble jets share the same pump and limited electrical power, activating the bubbles pauses the heating function until the massage cycle ends. That just means you’ll need to make sure the tub is at your desired temp before turning on the jets. This tub also isn’t rated for cold-weather use outdoors, so think of it as a fun addition to your warm-weather outdoor vibe.

There are two main types of hot tubs: plug-and-play models and hardwired spas. When we reached out to Courter, he recommended considering several factors before making a decision about which type of hot tub you should go for.

“The right choice depends less on preference and more on your setup, budget, and how much installation you’re willing to deal with,” says Courter. “There are many things specific to the hot tub being purchased. Things such as whether it is insulated, and what R-value does that insulation have?” R-value measures how well a hot tub’s insulation resists heat loss. The higher the R-value, the better it holds heat, and the less energy it uses to stay warm.

He notes that some hot tubs run on gas, though for this guide we’ve chosen only electric models. Where you live matters, too. “Ambient temperature will play a big part in operational costs,” he says. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain.”

Plug-and-play hot tubs are the easiest way in. Most run on a standard 110-volt outlet, so setup is straightforward. They require no electrician, no buried lines, and no major prep beyond a flat surface.

They’re typically made from molded plastic and are widely available online, which helps keep prices down. There are also some inflatable models on the market for less permanent use.

The trade-off, however, is performance. These models often have slower heating and less powerful jets compared with higher-end models. Still, for many homes (and especially rentals), this is the most practical option.

Hardwired spas require more planning. These usually run on 240 volts and need professional installation, but they deliver stronger jets, faster heating, and a more refined overall experience.

Most hardwired tubs have acrylic shells and insulated cabinets, which improves durability and efficiency. They also cost more upfront (and installation adds to that), but they feel closer to a traditional showroom spa experience.

If you’re worried about party-hosting capabilities, be wary. Capacity numbers can be misleading. A “six-person” tub will rarely feel comfortable with six adults. If you have the space, it’s usually worth sizing up.

A four-person model works well for one or two people who want room to stretch out, while six- or seven-person tubs are better for families or hosting. If you’re mainly using it for relaxation or hydrotherapy, a smaller tub is easier to maintain, and often more comfortable day to day.

Take time to think about jet count, but that’s not always a straightforward metric on which to judge a hot tub. What matters just as much is the placement, variety, and adjustability of those jets. Higher-powered pumps will provide stronger flow, as well. A lounger with carefully placed jets is a must if you’re seeking physical relief for aches and pains.

It’s fun to have perks like lights and sound systems, but those matter less than the features that keep a hot tub up and running for years. A good cover in particular makes a big difference. It helps retain heat, reduce energy use, and keep maintenance manageable.

But once you’ve chosen the size and key mechanical specs that meet your needs, it’s okay to jazz up the experience a bit with neat extras like waterfalls and lights. Just be mindful of additional maintenance. It’s easier to buy a new portable Bluetooth speaker than it is to repair one integrated into a hot tub.

Courter said that the exact operational cost is hard to guesstimate—a lot of factors come into play. “The longer a hot tub runs, the more expensive it is to maintain,” he says. “In Northern Utah, we can get down to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit in the wintertime. In that same timeframe, the average temperature in Miami is going to be in the mid-70s. A hot tub in northern Utah is going to need to run much more often to maintain its temperature.”

When it comes to chemicals and cost, that also varies depending on the size of the hot tub and how often you use it. General online user reports vary between $40 and $100 a month, but it’s not a number that’s easy to estimate. The initial setup will cost a bit more as you invest in the chemicals and supplies you’ll regularly need.

While hot tubs certainly are not a set-it-and-forget-it luxury, they are easier to maintain than a pool—and upkeep should not be a major deterrent. “Maintenance of a hot tub isn’t too bad if you stay on top of it,” says Courter. “Usually, it takes 10 to 20 minutes once a week to adjust your chemicals and clean your filters.”

When it comes to chemical options, whether you choose chlorine, bromine, copper, a salt system, or an ozone generator, they all work just fine—as long as you keep your pH in line. “A pH of 7 on the pH scale is neutral, but the pH of a human eye is 7.5, so I always suggest to my customers that they aim for around 7.5,” says Courter.

Other maintenance will involve keeping an eye on the water level, the condition of the hardware, and any signs of malfunction. Some hot tub repairs are simple and you can even DIY them, but many require calling an expert.

Other than structural considerations if you want it on an elevated deck, the options are virtually endless.

“A factory-built hot tub can go just about anywhere, as long as whatever you are putting it on can hold the weight,” says Courter. “A dry hot tub can weigh around 1,000 pounds, but remember that water weighs 8.34 pounds per gallon.” That means an average-sized spa could weigh nearly two tons.

When it comes to ground placement, a flat and level surface with a good base is fine for most uses. If you do choose to place a plug-and-play spa inside your home, be prepared to consult an expert about ways to mitigate moisture damage.

This is another one of those tricky metrics to guesstimate. We’ve listed the warranty windows for each tub we’ve included, but these spas should last longer than that.

“As with most items, it really depends on the quality of the product you buy,” says Courter. He says not all hot tubs are created equal and that consumer research goes a long way. That being said, spending more doesn’t guarantee a longer life for the hot tub.

“If a customer buys the highest-quality tub on the market and doesn't take care of it, it will fail quickly,” says Courter. “I have seen many hot tubs fail in just a couple of years if not maintained the way they should. In contrast, my wife and I still use a Watkins Hot Springs that is over 25 years old. Moral of the story: Buy the best quality that you can and take care of it.”

#6154. Vaping may disrupt the lung’s protective barrier after just one day

Experiments in human lung cells and hamsters suggest brief vaping exposure can disrupt protective barriers and leave lingering signs of cellular stress.

Vaping can seem easy on the lungs. New research suggests that even brief exposure can disrupt the cells that help them function.

Deep in the lung, where oxygen crosses into the blood, a single day of e-cigarette vapor was enough to injure the cells that line the smallest airways and blood vessels.

In hamsters exposed for five days, signs of cellular stress remained 10 days after exposure ended.

A separate experiment found changes in how previously exposed animals responded to a respiratory virus.

The work was done in human lung cells and tissue and in hamsters, not in people who vape. Irina Petrache, a lung specialist at National Jewish Health in Denver, was the senior author.

She is chief of the hospital’s Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, and researchers at the University of Colorado and Colorado State University took part.

“Our findings suggest that even short-term vaping exposure can initiate injury in the deepest and most delicate regions of the lung,” Petrache said.

“Importantly, some effects persisted after exposure ended and altered the immune response to a subsequent viral infection.”

The deep lung works because two thin sheets of cells stay sealed. One lines the smallest airways, and the other lines the tiny blood vessels wrapped around the air sacs.

Together, these layers allow oxygen to reach the blood while helping keep fluid out of the air spaces.

Petrache’s team worked with human cells of both kinds, some of them grown from donated lungs. They also used thin slices of lung from donors who had never smoked and had no lung disease.

The vapor came from a commercial product, JUUL pods in the Virginia Tobacco flavor with 5% nicotine. A machine puffed on the pods for three seconds every 30 seconds.

The researchers tested the vapor, the liquid, and the condensed aerosol at doses meant to mimic casual vaping.

Within a day, the cell sheets had begun to leak. The more vapor a sheet got, the more it leaked, and the highest dose did the most lasting damage.

A stressed cell runs a recycling program, breaking down its damaged parts and reusing the pieces.

Biologists call it autophagy, and it normally helps a cell survive and repair itself.

Vapor switched that program on, but the cells didn’t finish the job. Half-processed material piled up inside them. Their growth slowed, and some of the cells died.

The team traced the trouble to a stress signal inside the cell known as JNK.

When they gave the cells a drug that blocks JNK before the vapor arrived, the sheets held together better and the cleanup went further.

To examine whether the effects persisted in a living lung, the team turned to golden Syrian hamsters, whose small airways and responses to respiratory viruses resemble ours.

Six animals per group, male and female, breathed a mist made from the condensed vapor once a day for five days. Then they breathed clean air for 10 days.

By the end, the hamsters looked fine. They had not lost weight or shown signs of illness. Under the microscope, their lungs had no inflammation or scarring.

Inside the deep lung, the changes had not cleared. The marker of unfinished cleanup had risen about fourfold, and cells lining the small blood vessels carried broken strands of DNA.

About 200 genes were more active than in unexposed animals and about 300 were less active.

Some of the less active genes were associated with Th1 immunity, a branch of the immune system that helps fight viruses.

The authors wrote that many of those gene changes passed a loose statistical test but not a strict one, partly because each group held so few animals.

In 2019, an outbreak of severe lung injury hit people who used e-cigarettes, and the CDC counted more than 2,800 people hospitalized or dead from it.

A respiratory infection on top of the vaping was one suspected trigger. That outbreak is one reason the team tested what prior vaping does to an infected lung.

So a separate set of hamsters breathed the vapor mist for five days. Three days after the last dose, they received SARS-CoV-2 through the nose.

Some also received influenza A virus between the final vapor exposure and the SARS-CoV-2 infection.

In the first three days of infection, the exposed hamsters carried more SARS-CoV-2 in upper airway swabs than the unexposed ones.

A week in, their lungs showed less activity in antiviral genes and more in genes tied to breaking down and rebuilding lung tissue.

Sex made a difference. Exposed females lost more weight after infection than unexposed females, while exposed males lost less.

The inflammation and injury in the lung tissue itself showed no clear difference between the two groups.

None of this was measured in a person. Human cells in a dish and hamsters in a chamber can show what vapor does to tissue.

Studies of people who vape would need to establish whether similar changes occur in their lungs.

The team used one product in one flavor, and the hamsters breathed a condensate rather than fresh aerosol, a choice forced by biosafety rules at the time.

A condensate lacks the short-lived compounds in a fresh puff. The team also did not separate what nicotine did from what the flavoring or the other ingredients did.

Long-term lung diseases such as COPD, which narrows the airways, and fibrosis, which scars the lung, involve the same kind of leaky barrier.

The study cannot establish whether these early changes lead to chronic lung disease.

Future research could test whether blocking JNK limits the injury and whether similar changes occur in people who vape.

The full study was published in the journal JCI Insight.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6152. Mountains rise above a sea of clouds in the Pacific Northwest

A blanket of marine clouds covered the Pacific Northwest, leaving mountain peaks rising above the clouds like islands in the sky.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory captures a spectacular blanket of marine clouds stretching across the Pacific Northwest.

From space, the mountains appear to rise from a white sea.

A broad layer of low clouds covered much of western Washington and Oregon on September 19, 2026, stretching from the Pacific coast toward the foothills of the Cascade Range.

Only the higher terrain escaped the cloudy blanket. Peaks in Washington’s Olympic Mountains and parts of Oregon’s Coast Range poked through the clouds like islands.

NASA’s Terra satellite captured the striking scene at about 10:45 a.m. Pacific Time.

The image was captured by the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), an instrument aboard NASA’s Terra satellite that has observed Earth for more than two decades.

From orbit, MODIS can track clouds, smoke, vegetation, snow, ice, ocean conditions, and other features across large areas of the planet.

On this September morning, its view revealed just how far marine clouds had traveled inland.

Clouds also stretched far offshore over the Pacific Ocean.

Farther north, a different kind of haze appeared over the landscape as smoke from wildland fires collected in valleys of the North Cascades.

The widespread cloud cover over western Washington and Oregon resulted from cool, moist air moving inland from the ocean.

For several nights, marine air had been flowing onshore across the region.

This pattern can produce marine stratus – low, relatively uniform clouds that commonly develop along coastal areas.

The Pacific Ocean provides a huge source of moisture, while differences in temperature between the ocean, land, and atmosphere help determine where clouds form and how far they travel.

During the night and early morning, cool ocean air can move inland beneath warmer air higher in the atmosphere.

That arrangement creates what meteorologists call a temperature inversion.

Normally, air becomes colder with increasing altitude through the lower atmosphere. During an inversion, however, warmer air sits above cooler air near the surface.

The warmer layer acts like a lid, limiting the ability of the cooler air below to rise and mix with the atmosphere above.

When moist air trapped near the surface cools enough, water vapor condenses into tiny droplets. If enough droplets collect, a layer of stratus clouds develops.

The marine push was particularly strong during the early hours of September 19.

Cool, moist air reached well beyond the coastline, carrying clouds eastward until they approached the western foothills of the Cascades.

In some places, the cloud layer reached all the way to the ground.

At that point, what appears from space as a cloud becomes fog for people standing beneath it.

Clouds and fog are essentially the same phenomenon; the distinction largely depends on whether the suspended water droplets are touching the surface.

For residents below, the morning would have looked gray and muted. From hundreds of miles above Earth, however, the same weather pattern created a dramatic landscape.

Mountain summits rose through the smooth cloud deck while lower valleys and coastal terrain disappeared beneath it.

The Olympic Mountains offered one of the most striking examples.

Much of the lower terrain was hidden, leaving the tallest sections exposed above the cloud layer.

Similar features appeared along Oregon’s Coast Range.

Scenes like this also reveal how strongly topography shapes regional weather.

Mountains can redirect airflow, force air upward, influence rainfall, and help determine how far marine air penetrates inland.

The Cascades form an especially important barrier between the moist climate west of the range and the generally drier landscapes farther east.

On September 19, the marine layer had pushed far inland, but it did not last all day.

Several hours after Terra passed overhead, NASA’s Aqua satellite offered another look at the Pacific Northwest.

By about 4:15 p.m. Pacific Time, skies had cleared across much of western Washington and Oregon.

The transformation illustrates the daily rhythm of marine clouds.

As sunlight warms the land during the day, temperatures near the surface rise and atmospheric mixing increases. That process can weaken the inversion and break apart low clouds.

Yet the clearing was not complete. Some marine clouds remained pressed against the Oregon coast, where temperatures stayed cooler than they did farther inland.

The contrast captured during the day demonstrates how quickly coastal weather can change.

A landscape almost completely hidden beneath clouds in the morning can emerge only hours later.

From the ground, that shift might feel like an ordinary transition from a foggy morning to a sunny afternoon.

From orbit, it becomes something larger: an entire region briefly wrapped in a white blanket, with mountains rising above it like islands in the sky.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison

#6150. School playgrounds may have shade in all the wrong places

Researchers found that only one of nine playground areas met standards for shade, comfort, and play, raising questions about schoolyard design.

A shade sail stretched over a school playground looks like a job done. But children play where the fun is, not where the shade is.

When the two don’t line up, the shade covers an empty patch of ground while the children play in the sun.

Researchers in New Zealand have built a way of grading playgrounds that treats that mismatch as a design problem.

It scores every part of a schoolyard on whether it blocks the sun, whether it’s comfortable, and whether a child would want to play there.

On its first test, at a primary school in Christchurch, New Zealand, one of nine play areas passed.

Anupriya Sukumar of the School of Landscape Architecture at Lincoln University in New Zealand led the work. Her co-authors are at Lincoln and in the Department of Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning at Texas A&M University.

Sun protection is especially important in New Zealand. The country and neighboring Australia have the world’s highest rates of skin cancer, with about 100,000 New Zealanders affected each year.

Roughly a third of a person’s lifetime exposure to the sun comes before age 18.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sukumar said the schools she has mapped tend to put their shade in the wrong place.

“While shade was available in many schools, it was most commonly located around the perimeter of playgrounds, particularly along school boundaries,” she noted.

Those shaded strips often went underused, she said, because they weren’t where the children played.

Sukumar’s team starts by dividing a playground into activity zones, each one a place for a particular kind of play.

The Christchurch school had nine, from a sports field and a tennis court to a sandpit and a covered outdoor classroom.

Around each zone with a fixed purpose, the team drew a buffer of about 6.5 feet (2 meters) for the children waiting their turn.

Shade was measured for the worst moment of the school day. The team built a 3D model of the school and simulated its shadows for 1:30 p.m. on February 1.

That is the end of the summer lunch break, close to solar noon.

A zone passed on sun protection only if at least 80% of it was in shade dense enough to block most of the sun’s ultraviolet light for about an hour.

A thin tree canopy, which lets 70% of that light through, doesn’t count.

The surface underfoot reflects ultraviolet light back up at a child’s face.

Grass reflects about 2% of it and dry sand 20%, so a sunlit sandpit reflects ten times as much as a sunlit lawn. Asphalt and concrete fall in between.

The team assessed comfort separately, using five years of records from a nearby weather station to identify prevailing wind patterns.

They then mapped the areas sheltered from wind by buildings and trees.

Running children need shade with a breeze to stay comfortable, while children sitting down to eat need shade out of the wind. So each zone is scored against what happens there.

The third test is the simplest. A zone counts as attractive if it holds something that draws children in, such as climbing equipment, sand, or balls.

Only the covered outdoor classroom met all three tests. Four zones met one of them, and four met none. On sun protection alone, one zone was adequate, four were moderate, and four were low.

The sports field, the tennis court, and the basketball court all failed the attraction test.

School policy restricts balls at break time, so these large spaces lacked the equipment needed for their intended activities.

Asked what surprised her most, Sukumar singled out those big sports areas.

“One of the most surprising findings was that large portions of school playgrounds were dedicated to sports fields and hard courts, yet these spaces often lacked access to sports equipment, such as balls, due to lunchtime restrictions or school policies,” she said.

Smaller spaces such as sandpits and nature play areas took up much less of the playground, she said, and were often used more.

The grades lead to a repair plan the authors call the three Rs. A zone that nearly passes gets a retrofit, meaning a simple, low-cost change.

More serious failures call for a longer-term redesign. Schools can relocate or repurpose areas that fail every test and see little use.

A school can work through that list as money allows instead of rebuilding everything at once.

Sukumar told Earth.com that schools with funding for only one project this year should improve their busiest play area first.

The method was tried at one school, and the team hasn’t yet measured whether the children there spend more time in protected zones or get less sun.

“At this stage, we have not directly measured how much time children spend in shaded or sun-protected areas,” Sukumar said. “However, this represents an important next step for future research.”

The authors wrote that the attractiveness scores rest on what a zone contains rather than on watching children use it.

The pass marks come from earlier research, not from measurements at this school.

The comfort rules were set for Christchurch’s temperate climate and would need adjusting elsewhere, and the authors called the whole process complex and potentially time-consuming.

What would settle the open question is a count of where children actually go during outdoor play.

Sukumar said direct observation, or tracking children’s movements across a playground, could show whether the protected zones are used as intended and where shade is needed most.

The full study was published in the journal Cities & Health.
