#6137. The 8 Best Vacuums for Every Floor Type

I tried upright, cordless, canister, and robot vacs to find models that deliver reliable performance.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it comes to keeping your house clean, a reliable vacuum is a must. Vacuums are the quickest and easiest way to tackle dust bunnies, stubborn pet hair, and debris that collect in hidden corners. But not just any vacuum will do.

Finding the right vacuum is often overwhelming when you’re faced with sifting through dozens of upright models, robot vacuums, and more. A vacuum is a big investment, and an uninformed purchase often leads to disappointment if your choice turns out to be too heavy, too cumbersome, or not powerful enough. Plus, you want to pay for features you need without overspending on extras you’ll never use.

In this guide, we considered upright, cordless, canister, and robotic options from trusted brands, and evaluated them based on research and rigorous testing. We broke down key factors related to functionality, features, and maintenance to help you find the best vacuum, whether you need a pet-friendly option, one that’s powerful enough to clean up after kids, or a budget-friendly model.

More Home Appliances: Best Vacuums for Hardwood Floors • Best Dryers • Best Clothes Steamers

To find the best vacuums for every home, we first gathered a lineup of models across a range of brands, price points, and features. We deliberately chose a mix of canister, upright, stick, and robot vacuums to help ensure our selections accommodate different living situations, flooring types, and cleaning needs.

We focused on criteria like performance, ease of use, and versatility. For meaningful results, we ran each vacuum through a series of real-world tests to simulate common messes they’d be likely to come across in everyday life. We tried them on multiple surfaces like low-pile carpet, thick shag rugs, hardwood flooring, and bare concrete, seeing how well the vacuum adjusted to different demands. This also helped us assess suction power and how well the brush roll adapted to each surface type.

For debris, we chose materials that mimic typical household spills, like crumbled potato chips, popcorn, coffee, and cereal. The different weights and sizes of rubbish gave us a realistic view of how effectively the vacuum could remove the mess.

We also conducted similar tests with the handheld portions and attachments of these vacuums, using crevice tools and motorized brushes on couch cushions, on upholstery, and in tight corners. We noted how easy the tools were to maneuver, and whether they still packed enough power even when detached from the main unit.

By running each vacuum through comprehensive tests, we were able to get a clear picture of their real-world performance, so we could find dependable models for everyday cleaning.

I love using an upright vacuum for heavy-duty cleaning, and the AZ2002 packs the punch you need for tackling messes on carpets, couches, and floors. This model has two brushes: a soft roller brush and a foam-paddled brush. These work in tandem to increase contact with flooring and rugs, and I think that gives the vacuum a significant boost compared to models with just one traditional brush roll. The AZ2002 successfully picked up cat litter, dirt, and crumbs on a textured area rug.

All the cleaning modes are accessible right on the handle, so I was able to swiftly transition between carpet and laminate flooring without having to stop my cleaning session. The LED headlights brought attention to any dirt and gunk I missed during my initial swipes, too.

The AZ2002 also easily converts from an upright to a motorized canister vacuum. I especially liked using this functionality with the powered pet brush for cleaning couch cushions, so I didn’t have to haul the entire vacuum around. The hose and stick attachments extend to clean crevices and curtains, which I normally wouldn’t be able to reach.

The vacuum is on the heavier side, weighing a little over 16 pounds, but because it functions as a canister vac, I'm not too upset about sacrificing a little portability.

Full Shark AZ2002 Vertex Powered Lift-Away Upright Vacuum Review

I’ve had this vacuum from Shark for six years, and it has proved to be a reliable choice for apartments with hardwood, tile, area rugs, and two cats—so plenty of hair, litter, and dirt to go around.

I appreciate the Rocket for its lightweight build, convenient features, and usability. It transitions between hardwood and carpets using a switch right above the handle, and the base also detaches to become a handheld vacuum. The dustbin capacity is small, but that’s not uncommon for a stick vacuum. I just empty the dustbin whenever it gets too full by using the quick-release button.

The Rocket is easy to move around and underneath furniture, and it comes with useful attachments like a crevice tool, upholstery tool, and anti-allergen dusting brush for sucking up fine particles. The only bump in the road I’ve come across over the years is when I had a really shaggy carpet—the brush roll would often stop rotating and I’d have to untangle any fibers that got stuck.

You don’t get a ton of new tech with the Rocket, but I’ve found that it performs well on multiple surfaces. It also stores easily, and doesn’t require any hands-on effort emptying a bag or figuring out how to pair the appliance with a compatible app.

Full Shark HV301 Rocket Ultra-Light Corded Stick Vacuum Review

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser has a tangle-free brush roll, and even after using the vacuum on two large area rugs and hardwood floors, I didn’t find any hair wrapped in the bristles. What I did find, however, was plenty of pet hair, dirt, and dander in the dustbin because the suction power is strong enough to agitate carpet fibers and pick up debris that might not be completely visible.

I use the Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Hand Vacuum on an everyday basis, so I was excited to see that this upright model comes with a dedicated pet hair attachment for the hose wand. I tried it on my couch cushions, and a couple of pushes back and forth removed a majority of the mess. Plus, the canister detaches from the base so you can carry it around as you clean.

The vacuum only has two settings, plush carpet and low carpet/bare floor, so it isn't as versatile as other vacs for different floor types. But I liked being able to manually turn the brush roll on and off with a control switch on the base, which helped me tackle different cleaning tasks.

As a whole, this vacuum is a great option if you have allergies or pets. The combination canister-upright design adds maneuverability, and the attachments included are helpful for more intricate cleaning.

Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Allergen Lift-Off Upright Vacuum Review

When I think of canister vacuums, Miele comes to mind, and I’m willing to bet I’m not the only one. The brand is known for its powerful, well-designed canister vacuums, and the Classic C1 Turbo Team is, well, a classic.

It has six suction power settings, including options for hard floors, rugs, and even furniture. The floor head has a toggle switch that you can operate with your foot, switching between cleaning carpeting and hard floors easily.

The hose is long, which I found helpful because I didn’t have to lug the entire vacuum around as I cleaned. The cord is retractable, and the hose is completely detachable, so the C1 stores easily in a closet or laundry room. There’s also a removable component that holds the crevice tool and brushes.

The suction was impressive on low-pile carpets, but we wouldn’t suggest using this model on dense, thick carpets. The floor head also often lost suction during our tests. I particularly liked using this vacuum on furniture—it glided across the seat cushions, and the attachments came in handy for cleaning in between cracks and seams.

This style of vacuum captures dirt and other messes in self-sealing dust bags, so you’ll be able to clean for longer before needing to do any maintenance.

Full Miele Classic C1 Turbo Team Bagged Canister Vacuum Review

It might seem like cleaning is my favorite thing to do, given how many vacuums I’m testing regularly, but even I need a bit of a break sometimes. The Roborock Qrevo Series QV 35A has automated the process for me, so my weekly deep cleans don’t take nearly as long.

I have an 850-square-foot apartment, and it took about 30 minutes for the vacuum to map out my entire home. It worked its way over thresholds, across varied floor types, and in tight spaces with ease. I was impressed by how well it differentiated between carpet and hard flooring, so I didn’t have to worry about my area rugs getting wet during the mopping cycle.

It took 61 minutes for the QV 35A to vacuum my entire apartment. It worked around the perimeter first, and then moved in a zigzag pattern around the rest of the interior. There are a few different power options, and I ran it on turbo for most of the cleaning cycle because I have two pets. I felt like the suction power delivered, but it did kill the battery relatively quickly.

Mopping is equally as satisfying, and it took roughly half the time to do all my laminate floors. The QV 35A automatically refills and empties its water reservoir, so I don’t really have to do anything besides turn it on and let it do its thing.

The robot vacuum attempted to work its way over the legs of my kitchen island chairs, and after a few tries, it got stuck. Obstacle avoidance was mostly accurate otherwise, but I had to manually add a no-go zone in the app so the vacuum avoids this spot in the future.

Full Roborock Qrevo Series QV 35A Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

Dyson remains a top brand when it comes to cordless stick vacuums, and I’ve personally tested several of its models. The V15 Detect vacuum comes with a laser cleaner to illuminate hidden dirt, dust, and debris on hardwood floors, and this feature has proved to be very useful for me, even in well-lit rooms. The traditional-style cleaner head works well on carpet, and neither head feels lackluster in suction power.

The cordless-to-handheld structure is nice for going from longer cleaning sessions to quick or more detailed cleaning, and I like using the hair screw tool for removing pet fur from couches, cushions, and more. Better yet, there is a built-in dusting and crevice tool that is great for quick cleanups.

An LCD screen on the handheld portion shows what size of particles you’re cleaning up in real time, along with battery levels and overall cleanliness status. The HEPA filtration is added peace of mind that you’re getting a thorough clean.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

If a corded stick or upright vacuum isn’t the best choice for your home cleaning needs, then check out the LVAC-300 from Levoit. It’s a cordless stick vacuum that switches between hard floors, rugs, and tiles without skipping a beat or losing suction power. According to our tester, the vacuum uses three different modes to take on an array of cleaning jobs like picking up cat litter or fine dust, without spreading material around your floors.

It only weighs a little over 6 pounds, so it’s easy to lift and maneuver, and the vacuum lays completely flat for cleaning under furniture. The LED headlight on the floor head illuminates any lingering messes in areas with less visibility.

The LVAC-300 is designed with a five-stage HEPA filter with as much efficiency as an air purifier, and it’s also washable and reusable. The dust container releases with the touch of a button, and it empties just as easily.

We’re keen on the LVAC-300’s handheld vacuum capability and the various attachments it comes with, like a mini motorized brush for couch cushions and beds, and a crevice tool that is slender enough for car seats. A minor inconvenience is that there’s nowhere to store these accessories, which might occasionally interrupt your cleaning session if you have to change tools.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We recently added the Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum to our cleaning tool arsenal. It looks like something from the future, but it actually solves a lot of the problems cordless stick vacuums face in the present, namely when it comes to maneuverability and small-capacity dustbins.

The flexible center pole bends at a joint, which made it much easier for our tester to get under furniture and in tight spaces around his apartment. This vacuum uses detection technology to automatically adjust suction power based on the type of flooring and size of mess, so you don’t have to change manually and potentially miss spills or hidden debris. The floor head light helped illuminate dirt better, too.

Another useful feature is the docking station. Once our tester was finished cleaning, he locked the vacuum back onto the base, and it automatically suctioned collected dirt, hair, and dust out of the main dustbin. This doesn’t entirely offset the small dustbin capacity on the vacuum itself, but it’s nice not having to manually empty the receptacle after every clean.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We have several roundups of vacuums, including cordless stick models and robots. This guide is dedicated to the top overall vacuums we’ve tested, but there are still a few other units worth considering depending on your cleaning needs.

Miele Guard L1: This canister vacuum offers convenience and power for cleaning different floor types. The Classic C1 Turbo Team we recommend above comes with a powered carpet brush, while the L1 does not. It does have longer cable reach and an illuminated display, but the C1 is the better, more affordable selection if you have a mix of surface types in your home.

Shark PowerDetect: This is a buy-up version of the Shark PowerDetect Speed we recommend above. It comes with the same flexible hinge for cleaning under furniture and several intuitive features, including automatic suction adjustment and a cleaner head with LED lights for illuminating dirt. With the regular PowerDetect, you get 10 more minutes of run time and one more level of detection (the vacuum can tell when it’s in a corner or up against a wall and ramp up the suction accordingly). But you get more bang for your buck with the Speed.

Many vacuums are available in both corded and cordless models. Corded vacuums offer unlimited run time, but require a nearby outlet. Cordless or battery-powered models are convenient to use, as you can just pick them up and start cleaning, but they have a limited runtime.

The best option for you depends on how you like to clean—do you vacuum your whole house in one go? If so, go for a corded model. Or do you normally clean one room at a time? Then a cordless option might work just fine for your needs.

Different vacuums are better suited for cleaning hard floors or carpeting, and some feature heads that raise or lower to meet the height of the surface you’re vacuuming. If you have a combination of flooring types, you may want to look for a vacuum with multiple heads and attachments, too.

Vacuum brush rolls, or “beater bars,” come in several different styles, and each is made for specific cleaning tasks and flooring. The most common types you’ll see are bristle, soft, and tangle-free. Bristle rolls are designed with stiff, nylon bristles that are ideal for thick carpets because they lift dirt effectively. They are less optimal on delicate surfaces as their harsh structure causes scratches or other damage.

For hardwood floors, or homes with a mix of surfaces, a vacuum with a soft roll brush is what you need. They’re gentle yet efficient, picking up fine particles without scattering. Tangle-free is best for pet owners, since they resist hair wrapping and are easier to maintain.

Some of today’s vacuums feature dual brush rolls, or have detachable vacuum heads for adjusting to different situations.

Capacity refers to how much dust, dirt, and grime the vacuum can hold before the dustbin needs emptying. Bigger capacities are better for larger homes or heavy-duty cleaning, while smaller dustbins are better for compact spaces or low-lift tasks. Upright vacuums typically have a dustbin capacity of 0.75 liters or more, while stick vacs only hold a couple of quarts at a time.

Maneuverability determines how easily the vacuum navigates around furniture, corners, and other obstacles. Features like swivel steering, lightweight builds, and sturdy wheels all contribute to better control. Typically, vacuums with bigger capacity are more difficult to maneuver around, usually due to a combination of size and weight. Striking the right balance between capacity and maneuverability will help you find a vacuum that’s both efficient and easy to handle.

The suction power of vacuums is commonly measured in Pascals (Pa), a unit that gauges pressure, but some brands—including Dyson—list airwatts, or the watts used by the vacuum to move a unit of air through its nozzle, instead. Not all vacuums have their suction power listed, but when comparing different models, keep in mind that high Pa or airwatts equates to more suction power.

Vacuums vary widely in price ranging from as little as $20 to $1,000 or more. Budget-friendly vacuums tend to have less powerful suction and fewer features, and if it’s a cordless model, its battery life will likely be shorter. Premium vacuums, on the other hand, typically have an ergonomic design that’s more comfortable to operate for longer periods, and their suction power is often noticeably better.

While it’s certainly tempting to give up vacuuming all together, a robot vacuum generally isn’t going to be sufficient to keep your home clean. These vacuums are designed for light-duty cleaning, and they simply can’t match the suction power of a full-size vacuum, especially on carpeting. You might be able to get away with using just a robot vacuum if you have a small home, no pets, and solely hard floors, but I think you’d still find yourself needing another vacuum to clean up occasional messes.

If you have pets, you know that pet hair wreaks havoc on a vacuum. A few passes over a dirty rug, and all of a sudden there’s a wad of hair wrapped around the brush roll, forcing you to stop and untangle it. To avoid problems like this, I highly recommend vacuums designed for pet hair. These models often have anti-tangle brush rolls and good filters, ensuring they capture all the dirt and dander that your furry friends bring into your home.

While often neglected, vacuum cleaner maintenance is key to keeping your machine running properly and ensuring it will last for years to come. You’ll want to make sure you’re emptying the bag or dustbin as often as recommended, as well as washing or replacing filters. Periodically cleaning the brush roll improves suction power, too.

Some vacuums are easier to maintain than others, and you’ll want to be honest with yourself about how much maintenance you’re willing to do—otherwise, your expensive tool might break sooner than expected.

#6136. The Sky Today on Friday, November 6: Nab the North America Nebula

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

As fall gets into full swing, we are seeing less of the summertime stars. By 6 P.M. local time, the Summer Triangle — which flies high overhead on short summer nights — is now starting to set in the west. Lowest of its three points is Vega in Lyra; to Vega’s upper left is Altair in Aquila, while Deneb in Cygnus is almost directly above Vega and the highest of the three.

With no Moon in the sky, let’s use Deneb to find a favorite deep-sky object: NGC 7000, the North America Nebula. It’s a great small scope target, and its location just 3° east of Deneb makes it easy to center in the eyepiece. However, this huge emission nebula stretches about 2° across, so note that it requires a larger field of view to capture all in one go. It definitely benefits from a nebula filter if you have one.

On the sky, the nebula’s western side looks like the eastern coast of the continent for which it is named, and vice versa. The curve that mimics the Gulf of Mexico is particularly prominent, so start there if you’re having trouble seeing the shape. Look also to NGC 7000’s west — across a dark gulf, you’ll see a fainter, more compact patch of nebulosity. This is IC 5067/5070, also known as the Pelican Nebula.

Sunrise: 6:35 A.M.Sunset: 4:52 P.M.Moonrise: 3:56 A.M.Moonset: 3:16 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

#6135. Women who used menopause hormone therapy had less brain vessel damage later in life

Women who had used menopause hormone therapy showed fewer signs of damage to small brain blood vessels at 70.

Estrogen helps regulate the menstrual cycle and supports pregnancy, but it also helps keep blood vessels healthy, including those in the brain.

That second job may still matter decades after menopause.

Women who had used menopause hormone therapy showed fewer signs of damage to the brain’s smallest blood vessels at age 70.

Women whose menopause came later showed a similar but weaker pattern.

Damage to these tiny vessels becomes more common with age, and it’s linked to a higher chance of stroke and dementia.

Giulia Lorenzon, now at the Yale School of Medicine, and Anna Marseglia of Karolinska Institutet in Sweden led the work.

The team compared each woman’s hormone history with her brain scans but never gave anyone hormones, so the study can show links but can’t prove cause and effect.

Doctors use the word cerebrovascular to describe the brain’s blood vessels.

“Our results suggest that hormonal exposure across different periods of a woman’s life may have cumulative effects also on the cerebrovascular health in later life,” said Marseglia, one of the study’s senior authors.

“The findings suggest that the brain’s blood vessels may play an important role in the link between estrogen and brain aging.”

The women all took part in the Gothenburg H70 Birth Cohort Studies, a long-running study of aging in Gothenburg, Sweden. Between 2014 and 2016, 352 women born in 1944 had MRI brain scans at about age 70.

None had dementia. On a common 30-point test of memory and thinking, the women averaged just over 29.

Staff asked each woman about her reproductive history and used her answers to work out her reproductive span, the number of years between her first period and menopause.

A woman whose first period came at age 13 and whose menopause came at age 50, for example, had a span of 37 years. That’s close to the group’s average.

The ovaries make most of a woman’s estrogen. For women who had both ovaries removed, the researchers used their age at surgery to calculate their reproductive span.

Most of the women had also used hormones. About 73% had taken birth control pills, and about 61% had used menopause hormone therapy.

That level of hormone use fits Swedish history, the authors wrote. The pill caught on in the mid-1960s, and hormone therapy use rose sharply in the 1990s, as these women reached menopause.

The brain depends on a dense network of small blood vessels. Damage to them is called small vessel disease, and it often causes no symptoms, so many people learn they have it only from a brain scan.

Radiologists checked each scan for four common signs. Large bright patches in the brain’s white matter can mark areas where blood supply has suffered.

Lacunes are small holes often left behind by tiny strokes, and microbleeds are pinpoint spots of old bleeding.

The fourth sign is widened fluid-filled spaces around the vessels themselves.

Each woman got one point for each sign that passed a set threshold. About 59% of the women scored zero, and 12% scored two or more. No one scored four.

The team also measured the white matter itself, the bundles of nerve fibers that carry signals between brain areas.

In healthy white matter, water tends to move along nerve fibers rather than across them. The scans measured this movement to assess the tissue’s structure.

Women with more years between their first period and menopause were less likely to score two or more. Each extra year was tied to about 8% lower odds of that higher score.

The team found the same pattern after accounting for education, pregnancies, and breastfeeding.

The age at menopause mattered more than the age at a first period. A later menopause was tied to a lower score and to fewer lacunes.

Still, this was one of the weaker results. When researchers run dozens of comparisons, a few can look real by luck alone, so the team applied a stricter test that allows for that.

The reproductive span link weakened under that test, and it weakened again when the team left out the 31 women who’d had a stroke or a mini-stroke.

Women who had used menopause hormone therapy had less than half the odds of scoring two or more, compared with women who never had. Their white matter also looked more orderly.

Both of those links passed the stricter test. They held after the team accounted for high blood pressure, heart disease, and diabetes, and when women with a past stroke were left out.

Birth control pill use was linked to more orderly white matter but not to a lower score, and that white matter link faded under the stricter test.

Women who had used birth control pills when younger and menopause hormone therapy later had the most favorable scans.

Compared with women who had used neither, they had about a third of the odds of scoring two or more.

The researchers found no clear interaction between birth control pill use and menopause hormone therapy.

They described the combined pattern as preliminary and called for studies in more varied groups of women.

Women make up about two-thirds of dementia cases. Earlier studies of hormone therapy and dementia have reached opposite conclusions, with some finding lower risk and others higher.

So the team also measured four areas of the brain that tend to thin early in Alzheimer’s disease. Overall, none of the hormone measures was linked to the thickness of those areas.

One exception involved a version of a gene called APOE. Its ε4 version raises the risk of Alzheimer’s, and about a third of the women carried at least one copy.

Among those carriers, hormone therapy users had thicker tissue in the Alzheimer’s-prone areas than nonusers. That result didn’t pass the stricter test, and the authors wrote that it should be read with caution.

Among the 205 women scanned again five years later, hormone history made no clear difference to how fast the bright patches grew or the Alzheimer’s-prone areas thinned.

Hormone therapy users had a hint of slower growth in the bright patches, but it wasn’t strong enough to rule out chance.

To the authors, the split between these results suggests that estrogen’s link to brain aging in these women may mostly involve the blood vessels.

The women recalled their hormone use decades later, and researchers recorded whether they had used birth control pills or menopause hormone therapy.

The study didn’t capture the products, doses, or treatment start dates.

“Furthermore, the study is an observational study, and we cannot therefore determine cause and effect,” Lorenzon said. “The results cannot therefore be used as a basis for recommending hormone therapy for preventive purposes.”

The volunteers were also a healthy, well-educated group from one city.

Among the women with white matter measurements, only 46 had used neither the pill nor hormone therapy, so that comparison group was small.

Some earlier research suggests hormone therapy may help the brain most when it starts close to menopause.

The team couldn’t test that idea, because the study didn’t record when each woman began.

Nor did the researchers check whether healthier-looking vessels made any difference to memory or thinking.

Answering that will take studies that record exactly which hormones women took and when, then follow their thinking skills along with their brain scans.

The full study was published in the journal Neurology.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6133. A honey bee’s stinger keeps pumping venom after the bee flies off, and now scientists know how

Video shows that a honey bee stinger works as a tiny, double-piston pump, with collapsing valves that keep pushing venom after the bee has gone.

A honey bee stings once, leaves its stinger in your skin, and flies off to die. It looks like the end of the attack. It isn’t.

The stinger left behind is a self-contained unit, with its own venom sac, muscles and nerves. It keeps digging in and pumping venom on its own after the bee has gone.

Scientists have now filmed that happening at high speed. Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel of Macquarie University in Sydney and her colleagues watched detached stingers push into a clear gel that stands in for skin. The gel is not living tissue, but it lets a camera see what skin would hide.

The stinger, they found, works as a pump but is unlike most pumps that people build: two flexible pistons sliding in opposite directions inside a single chamber.

“We’ve known since as early as 1910 that the venom sac of a honey bee stinger empties into a chamber with little pumping elements called valves, but until now we didn’t know exactly how they work,” said Ramirez-Esquivel.

The honey bee is one of only a handful of insects whose stinger is built to tear away from its body. When the bee pulls free, the stinger stays put, along with its venom sac, several glands, a cluster of nerve cells, and the muscles that drive it.

The team, from Macquarie and UNSW Canberra, took stingers from live worker bees. Each tip went into a small block of clear gel about a sixth of an inch (4 millimeters) long.

A stinger is partly see-through, so a strong light shone through it let cameras running at up to 500 frames a second record the parts moving inside.

The stinger only pumped properly when it had something to push into. Without gel, its pumping parts barely moved. In the gel, strong pumping lasted from 15 seconds to just over a minute in a sample of 10 stingers.

It then faded to twitches that went on for two to five additional minutes. In an interview with Earth.com, Ramirez-Esquivel said the speed of the stinging made it hard to film.

“There is no time to adjust, you either catch it or you don’t,” she said. “I still did not expect the sheer number of attempts we had to go through to capture this footage.”

Inside the stinger, the venom sac empties into a small chamber at the base. Two long, sharp blades called lancets slide back and forth through that chamber along a rail.

Their backward-facing barbs anchor the stinger in skin and work it deeper with each stroke. Scorpions and spiders deliver venom differently, by squeezing muscles around a venom gland.

Each lancet carries a small, flexible flap, called a valve, inside the chamber. The two valves move in opposite directions: when one travels down toward the tip, the other travels up.

A single stroke moves a valve about a sixtieth of an inch (0.45 millimeters), roughly the thickness of four sheets of paper, in about seven tenths of a second. The venom then leaves through a canal about half the width of a human hair.

On the downstroke, each valve inflates like a parachute and pushes venom ahead of it. On the upstroke it collapses, so venom can flow past it and refill the chamber below while the other valve is pushing.

The top of the chamber is also wider than the valves can seal, which leaves a space where fresh venom keeps entering even while pumping goes on.

Then the two valves meet. “Finally, and perhaps most dramatically, as the valves meet in the middle of the stroke, they change shape again to push past each other,” said Ramirez-Esquivel.

“This is a remarkable strategy to pump fluid since maintaining a seal is vital to transmit pressure effectively.”

There are no muscles inside the chamber or the valves, so every change of shape is passive.

To test the idea, the team scanned stingers from a Canberra hive at the Australian National University and 3D printed a scaled-up chamber with flexible plastic valves pumping glycerol. Its valves moved like the real ones.

A syringe shows why that matters. Its one rigid piston can’t refill without pulling back, so it can’t deliver a steady flow. The stinger’s two collapsing pistons pump and refill at once.

“The stinger pump design is quite unusual in having two pistons in a single pumping chamber,” Ramirez-Esquivel told Earth.com.

She said that, as manufacturing advances, the design may become practical to produce at scale for uses such as medical pumps for drug delivery.

The stinger has already inspired microneedle designs, and mosquito mouthparts have inspired 3D printing nozzles.

Asked by Earth.com the best way to remove a stinger, Ramirez-Esquivel said the stinger empties the venom sac within about 30 seconds to two minutes.

Taking it out as quickly as possible limits how much venom gets into the skin, she said. Near a hive, though, it is better to get away calmly and quickly first.

The reason is in the stinger itself. It carries glands that release alarm pheromones, chemical signals that recruit other bees to sting. “If there is something worse than getting stung once it is getting stung multiple times,” she said.

The stinger’s independence also makes sense for the bee. A worker that leaves its stinger behind dies, but the stinger keeps delivering venom whether or not the bee survives.

The authors wrote that this suits an insect that defends its colony with its life.

The team could not directly see venom flowing inside the chamber. The refill space at the top is inferred from the shapes and timing of the valves.

Whether the collapsing valve fully stops venom from being sucked back up is also unknown, and the authors wrote that more work is needed to measure that.

How the valves squeeze past each other is unresolved too. The video suggests the cup-shaped part of each valve collapses sideways, while in the printed model the valve’s wings flipped upward. The authors wrote that future work is needed to settle which happens in the real stinger.

In addition, the authors have not measured what the valves are made of, because each one is small and fragile enough to damage on removal. And every stinger was filmed in gel, not living skin.

The next step the authors proposed is to freeze stingers in liquid nitrogen in mid-sting and scan them, catching the valves in whatever shape they take as they pass.

The scans from this study are public on MorphoSource for anyone who wants to look.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6132. Nov. 6, 1919: Einstein is right

The earliest test of Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity took place just four years after he published it. During the May 29, 1919, total solar eclipse, British astronomer Sir Arthur Eddington and colleagues studied the theory by measuring how the Sun distorts light from background stars.

According to general relativity, any object with mass warps space-time. (The common analogy is that it’s similar to a bowling ball on a trampoline.) So, any passing body will follow a curved trajectory; this is true whether the passing body is an orbiting satellite or a light photon from a background object.

Researchers involved with the 1919 eclipse expedition traveled to two locations to observe totality: northern Brazil and a western island of Africa. According to general relativity, the apparent positions of stars near the Sun would appear to shift by 1.75 arcseconds. The scientists first measured the positions of stars in the Hydra star cluster in early 1919. Eddington and colleagues then recorded the stars’ locations during totality, and compared them to the previous values. They found that indeed, the background stars appeared to shift by roughly the amount general relativity had predicted. (They measured 1.98 arcseconds and 1.61 arcseconds.) The researchers announced their data on Nov. 6, 1919, and Einstein quickly became a household name.

Liz Kruesi is science writer with a background in physics who specializes in astronomy and space-related news.

#6131. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

#6130. When eco-friendly advertising backfires: More green claims can make a product less appealing

Advertising both eco-friendly ingredients and sustainable packaging can lower a product’s appeal among shoppers who care less about buying green.

A product made with eco-friendly ingredients and sold in sustainable packaging sounds like an easy sell.

But a new study suggests that advertising both benefits can make it less appealing to some shoppers.

People who care a lot about buying green rated a product higher when its ad mentioned both. People who care less rated it higher when the ad stuck to just one.

At least with these ads, more green information wasn’t automatically more persuasive.

Miyuri Shirai, a professor at Keio University, tested this in three experiments with 1,729 people in Japan. The products were made up for the study, and people rated ads instead of buying anything.

Soap, cereal, detergent and other things people buy over and over are called consumer packaged goods. A growing number of them are sold as better for the planet.

In 2023, 18.5% of these goods sold in the US were marketed as sustainable, according to the NYU Stern Center for Sustainable Business. That’s up 4.8 percentage points from 2015.

McKinsey & Company and NielsenIQ found that products with sustainability claims grew their sales by 28% over five years, compared with 20% for products without those claims.

Growth like that leaves companies with a choice. They can make the product itself greener by changing what goes into it or how it’s made. Or they can work on the packaging, using better materials, a new design or a package that can be recycled.

Sustainable packaging gets a lot of attention because these products are bought and thrown away so often. All that packaging uses up raw materials and energy and adds to pollution.

Doing both often costs more and makes production harder. So it helps to know whether shoppers actually reward the extra effort.

At first glance, two green features should beat one. Researchers call this the more-is-better pattern, where the more good things an ad says about a product, the better people tend to rate it.

A much older finding suggests otherwise. In a 1992 study, Daniel Kahneman and Jack Knetsch looked at how much people were willing to pay for environmental services.

People tended to value something less when it came as part of a bigger package than when it was judged on its own. This is called the embedding effect, and it’s where Shirai’s question started.

“My interest in this research began when I read articles about the embedding effect, which suggest that adding more positive information does not always make an option seem better,” Shirai said.

“I became curious about whether communicating multiple sustainability benefits might sometimes be less effective than highlighting just one, depending on the consumer,” she added.

At Keio’s Faculty of Business and Commerce, Shirai studies the psychology of how shoppers judge products. For this project, she recruited people through Freeasy, a Japanese online survey panel.

Each person saw one ad for a made-up product. Some ads talked only about what the product was made of, others only about the packaging, and the rest about both.

People then rated the product. Shirai also measured how much each person cares about buying things that are good for the environment, which researchers call green consumption values.

The first experiment used laundry detergent. Of the 750 people recruited, 124 failed a check meant to catch careless answers, which left 626.

The second used organic granola, a food that’s widely sold and already seen as sustainable.

Switching from detergent to food helped test whether the pattern held across different product categories.

This time, 600 of the 750 recruits made it through the same check.

Body wash was the product in the third experiment, which included 503 people. Those people also answered extra questions to help explain why they reacted the way they did.

In all three experiments, the results came out the same way.

People who cared more about green buying rated the product higher when the ad covered both the product and its packaging than when it covered only one.

People who cared less did the reverse. They rated the product higher when the ad stuck to a single feature.

That second group’s response was consistent with the embedding effect.

For them, one green feature may have seemed less impressive when it came bundled with another.

For the first group, Shirai had a different explanation. It’s hard to tell how green a product really is from an ad or a label, so people look for small clues.

For someone who cares a lot about the environment, details about the product and details about its package may work as two clues that back each other up.

“Emphasizing sustainability in both the product and its packaging may not always be the most effective strategy,” she said.

In the body wash experiment, people also rated how useful they found the green information and how sustainable they thought the product was.

Both ratings were linked to how people felt about the product, and those links depended on each person’s green values.

The analysis couldn’t show which came first, though, so this is a possible explanation rather than proof.

There’s one catch in how the ads were built.

The ads that mentioned both the product and its packaging had four green statements, while the single-focus ads had two each.

So the results can’t show for sure what people were reacting to. It could have been the number of claims, or whether the claims covered one feature or two.

Everyone in the study was in Japan, and participants rated fictional products without spending real money.

Whether tailoring ads to shoppers’ green values would increase sales or benefit the environment remains untested.

The full study was published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology.

#6129. Permafrost Is Thawing From the Inside Out—and It’s Unleashing an Entirely New Kind of Landslide

Wildfires from decades ago may be secretly melting the frozen ground from below, setting off a disastrous chain of events in the present.

The largest northward-flowing river in North America, Canada’s Mackenzie River carries roughly 78 cubic miles of freshwater out of Great Slave Lake, winds through the frozen expanse and pristine forests of the Northwest Territories, and eventually empties into the Beaufort Sea, a marginal sea of the larger Arctic Ocean. The river represents the second-largest drainage basin on the continent, covering roughly 20 percent of Canada’s total landmass. The river valley served as the ancestral home of the Dene people, who in Slavey (a group of Athabaskan languages) called the river dehcho, or simply “big river.”

For thousands of years before the arrival of industrial revolution, permafrost—soil, rock, and sediment that stays frozen at least two consecutive years—encased this part of the world in frozen beauty. But with rising anthropogenic carbon emissions, that immemorial stability is crumbling away. And in some places in the central Mackenzie Valley, melting permafrost is changing the landscape in surprising ways.

In 2017 and 2018, two gargantuan landslides impacted the area, moving 4.5 and 18 million cubic meters of frozen ground respectively. Landslides, on their own, aren’t necessarily surprising. As the climate warms and permafrost thaws, boreal and tundra ecosystems, whether in Canada, Alaska, or other northern regions of the world, have seen an increasing risk of landslides. However, the leftover evidence of these huge terrestrial deluges raised a few questions, chiefly because they appeared to carry large chunks of frozen ground with them.

In 2019, permafrost geologist Joseph Young, then with the University of Alberta as a Ph.D. student, traveled by helicopter to a remote field site when he spotted slopes “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” he told Science News. Young admits he was puzzled by these particular landslides because permafrost typically melts from the top down, making a muddy slurry that forms a slow-moving landslide.

However, the Mackenzie Valley landslides contained chunks of still-frozen earth that had moved hundreds of meters, and initial ground observations showed that sliding occurred roughly 20 meters under the top layer of permafrost. To better understand the mechanics of this strange landslide formation, Young and a team of researchers from the University of Alberta set up instruments to track ground temperature from 2020 until 2022. They hypothesized that wildfires—including some that occurred decades in the past—and rising summer temperatures formed tension cracks, allowing water to seep in and cause the permafrost to thaw from below. They called this new kind of landslide “permafrost detachment slides” and reported their observations in the journal Geophysical Research Letters.

“Climate warming and wildfire work together to drive heat to depth over decades, weakening the permafrost base,” the authors wrote. “Exposed ice-rich scarps continue thawing, triggering secondary landslides and irreversibly reshaping the landscape.”

Melting permafrost isn’t just rearranging these long-standing slopes, it's also unleashing previously trapped metals into riverbeds, turning them in some cases a bright, eye-popping orange. Shifting permafrost is also swallowing up villages in Alaska’s remote tundra, and studies estimate that continued thawing could cause upwards of $50 billion in damage to buildings and roads in Alaska by 2050.

The impact of climate change can’t be ignored, from rising sea levels inundating coastal communities to roiling wildfires that blanket world-renowned cities in smoke. And in the coldest regions of the world, climate change is quite literally changing the ground beneath our feet.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6128. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 7: Venus meets the Moon

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Venus is already primed to capture attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

#6126. Construction crews in California accidentally unearthed the bones of a large mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago

Fossils found during construction in Oceanside, California, may belong to a giant hoofed mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago.

During routine excavation for a city infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, Joseph El Adli, a principal paleontologist with Helix Environmental Planning, spotted fossil bones about 12 feet (3.7 meters) below the surface. He recognized their importance and secured the area.

The bones belong to a large, hoofed mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago, the City of Oceanside announced on September 22, 2026.

The animal may be a titanothere, nicknamed “thunder beast,” or Amynodon, historically called a “swamp rhino.” Laboratory work should settle which.

He was monitoring the dig as the project’s paleontologist. The city places monitors on major infrastructure work as standard practice and to comply with California environmental laws.

The find includes several limb bones, ribs and numerous other bones and fragments. The largest piece appears to be a femur.

El Adli’s team worked for seven days to expose the bones from beneath several tons of hardened mudstone and sandstone.

The fossils were then wrapped in a plaster field jacket and moved to an off-site laboratory.

The exact location has not been disclosed, to protect public safety and the integrity of the site.

The bones came from Member C of the Santiago Formation, a thick sequence of sedimentary rock in northwestern San Diego County.

Paleontologists based the age estimate on the known age of that rock and the types of organisms found in it. The range falls within the Eocene Epoch, in a stretch of time called the Uintan North American Land Mammal Age.

According to the city, the animal roamed ancient floodplains in the area.

The same rock unit in the city has yielded Diegoaelurus vanvalkenburghae, a predator named in a 2022 description of Diegoaelurus. It belongs to the machaeroidines, the oldest group of sabertooth mammals.

Known from a nearly complete lower jaw with most of its teeth, it is the youngest machaeroidine on record. Its authors tentatively tie the group’s extinction to faunal change at the shift from the middle to the late Eocene, part of a wider turnover among mammal predators.

The fossil site that produced it, known as Jeff’s Discovery, also holds a tapir relative called Hesperaletes and a hyaenodontid predator, Limnocyon.

The paper was led by Shawn Zack of the University of Arizona College of Medicine in Phoenix, with Ashley Poust of the San Diego Natural History Museum.

Both candidates belong to Perissodactyla, the order of odd-toed hoofed mammals that includes today’s horses, rhinos and tapirs. Titanotheres are also known as brontotheres.

Oceanside officials describe them as animals roughly the size of a black rhino, with deep chests, a distinct shoulder hump and small horns.

In 2001, paleontologists collected brontothere remains from a sandstone layer at another construction site in Oceanside, near Rancho del Oro Road.

That animal, Parvicornus, stood about 5 to 6 feet (1.5 to 1.8 meters) at the shoulder, according to the San Diego Natural History Museum. It had only a very small horn, more of a bump, near each eye.

Brontotheres began as dog-size animals in the early Eocene and grew larger over roughly 20 million years. Those in South Dakota’s Badlands, about 38 to 34 million years ago, reached around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and 16 feet (4.9 meters) long.

The Badlands animals carried blunt, paired horns on their noses, sometimes more than 3.3 feet (1 meter) long. Males had larger horns than females.

These herbivores most likely ate soft leaves in Eocene forests. The group died out at the end of the Eocene, likely as the climate turned cooler and drier, the National Park Service notes.

Amynodon is the namesake of the amynodonts, which the American Museum of Natural History describes as large-bodied, hornless rhinos. Amynodon itself had a squat, hippo-like body, city officials say.

Their nickname comes from an older idea that they spent much of their time in water. Evidence for that is very limited.

Only Metamynodon, the last North American amynodont, may have been semi-aquatic. Its fossils turn up in sandstone laid down by rivers.

Amynodonts lived in Asia and North America from the middle Eocene through the early Oligocene. They have no living relatives and sit far from today’s species on the rhino family tree.

Amynodon had a large hollow in the skull in front of each eye socket. It likely anchored muscles for an enlarged upper lip.

At the laboratory, preparators will remove the plaster jackets. They will then harden and stabilize the fossils with museum-grade glues and resins.

Once the bones are fully freed from the surrounding rock, paleontologists expect to narrow down the animal’s precise identity.

The specimens are expected to join a museum collection, where they will be preserved and available to scientists and the public. The museum has not been named.

Several jacketed blocks have not been opened yet, and a skull may be inside one of them.

The information was obtained from the City of Oceanside.

#6125. Nov. 7, 1882: A Great Comet transforms astrophotography

In early September 1882, a comet was sighted from the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. The comet brightened over the following weeks, reaching a magnitude of -2 on the 15th; at perihelion two days later, it was bright enough to be visible during the day. But at the time, David Gill, the director of the Cape Observatory, was busy observing minor planets Victoria and Sappho. It wasn’t until Oct. 12 that, his minor planet observations completed, he turned his attention to the comet and began photographing it.

Gill captured images of the Great Comet of 1882 on Oct. 12, 20, and 21, and Nov. 7, 13, and 14. The Nov. 7 shot was the one he would become famous for, though: It was not the first photograph of a comet, but rather would signal a change in astronomers’ uses of astrophotography. The photo was a 100-minute exposure, resulting an image that included stars to 10th magnitude and the comet’s 18-degree tail. Spurred by the large number of stars captured in his photo, Gill saw the potential for using astrophotography for star mapping and began the Cape Photographic Durchmusterung. (Durchmusterung means “close examination” or “scrutiny.”) The project would catalog nearly a half-million southern stars. Gill shared the successes of the program internationally, prompting the assembly of the world’s first major astronomical conference. As a result, astronomers worldwide began to move away from traditional, manual star mapping and towards more efficient and comprehensive photographic techniques.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6124. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.
