#6050. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

Whether you already have a stockpile of United MileagePlus miles or are taking advantage of the great welcome bonuses on offer right now on United Airlines credit cards, we have some incredible ways to use those miles on your next adventure.

Right now, you can earn as many as 90,000 United miles by applying for one of several offers from Chase and United Airlines and meeting the minimum spend requirements.

Using the United website and award search tools like Point.me, Seats.aero and Points Path, here are 10 standout ways you can redeem a big stash of United miles. And if you have a United credit card, elite status or both, keep an eye out for even better deals, as some of the awards you're considering may offer additional savings.

One of my favorite recent redemptions was my first-ever United Polaris flight from Tokyo's Haneda Airport (HND) to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) — before continuing on to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) — for just 80,000 United MileagePlus miles plus $5.60 in taxes and fees. What a screaming deal!

While I didn't find that exact flight while conducting more recent searches, I did find a flight in Polaris from Tokyo's Narita International Airport (NRT) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) —and then on to EWR in economy — for 85,000 United MileagePlus miles plus $63.19 in taxes and fees. The cash rate for a similar itinerary would be $8,057.

Related: Everything you need to know about United Polaris business class

You can fly to or from Europe for as few as 68,000 United MileagePlus miles one-way in United Polaris business class. That's a great deal. Availability comes and goes, but I was able to find plenty of dates with the lowest-level saver fares. Cardmembers save 66% on this redemption.

Note that you can also fly on one of United's European partners, such as Lufthansa or ITA Airways. Here's an example flight from Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci Airport (FCO) to EWR for 80,000 miles and $110.19 in taxes and fees. As a noncardholder, you'd pay 200,000 miles.

How does London sound with your new stash of United miles? There is usually sporadic availability to and from London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) for as low as 68,000 miles (but watch out for those onerous taxes of more than $432). That compares to a cash fare of $2,747, so you'll still save a sizable amount by booking with miles, even after accounting for the higher fees.

This week, we found a business-class flight on United from EWR to Johannesburg's O.R. Tambo International Airport (JNB) for as few as 68,000 miles plus $5.60 in taxes and fees. That fare didn't last long, but another search found multiple days with business class for just 80,000 miles.

That's nearly 15 hours in lie-flat United Polaris heaven. What a great deal! Those prices are not common, but it does give you an idea of what's possible. And check out how much we saved by booking as a cardmember.

Earlier this year, we found business-class fares from Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) to San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and then on to LAX for just 90,000 United MileagePlus miles and $74.23 in taxes and fees. That's the long flight in United's brand-new, next-generation Polaris business-class product, making it an exceptional deal considering a similar one-way flight this winter costs about $3,767.

Related: Spacious suites and fine wines: A review of United's new Elevated Polaris business class

It's a similar find for the long flight from Sydney Airport (SYD) to SFO or LAX.

I found multiple days with redemptions for just 85,000 United MileagePlus miles plus $104.29 in taxes and fees. Again, you'd be in United's new business-class product. The cash price is $4,871 for that same flight. As a cardmember, you'd save 79% compared to noncardholders for that same award.

Related: Complete guide to United’s revenue, award and upgrade fare classes

You would have enough miles to fly a family of three round-trip from California all the way across the country in economy for just 12,700 miles each way per passenger. That's a total of 76,200 miles and $33.60 in taxes and fees for the round-trip itinerary. The cash price would be $1,649.10, while noncardholders booking with miles would pay 15,000 miles each way per person (or 15% more).

Related: How a United credit card can save you hundreds of thousands of miles on flights

How does a trip to Hawaii sound? You can use your stockpile of United MileagePlus miles to fly round-trip to paradise.

We found flights from EWR to Honolulu's Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) for just 42,400 United miles round-trip (plus $11.20 in taxes and fees). That means you could bring a friend, too, for just 84,800 miles and $22.40 in taxes and fees — or the miles you'd earn from a welcome bonus on one credit card. A similar two-week trip booked with cash would be more than $2,621.

Related: Cool things for the rest of us: 6 innovations United Airlines is bringing to its economy cabins

You can also fly to Hawaii in United first class using your stash of United miles.

Fly from SFO to HNL for just 56,600 miles plus $5.60 in taxes and fees. While you wouldn't have enough for a round-trip flight, you could fly round-trip in coach for just 18,800 miles each way.

Here's a fun flight I found on Point.me. You can use your United MileagePlus miles to fly from New York to Brussels and then on to Accra, Ghana, for just 88,000 United miles. It's a flight I've previously flown for a PeaceJam trip to Ghana.

By having a United Airlines credit card and booking through the United website, you'll redeem even fewer miles for the same flight. Booking this way requires only 80,000 miles plus $102.20 in taxes and fees, saving cardmembers 9%.

There's one other unique redemption to tell you about. United has what it calls "United MileagePlus Exclusives," which offer some unique items you can bid on.

You can bid on experiences like a Broadway show, a holiday trip to Waikiki from Marriott Bonvoy and a game of flag football with the New York Giants. Your miles could unlock some pretty cool adventures, no matter how you spend them.

United MileagePlus miles can unlock some incredible travel deals, especially if you're willing to be flexible with your travel dates and destinations.

As our searches show, you can get tremendous value from your miles, whether you're booking a lie-flat business-class seat to Europe, Asia or Africa or taking the whole family to Hawaii.

The key is to compare award prices with cash fares, search multiple dates and take advantage of the additional award availability and discounts offered to eligible United credit card holders and elite members.

#6048. Christmas Flights To Europe Cost $2,000 Each In Economy. Should I Book Now Or Gamble On Award Space?

I’m faced with a travel dilemma concerning holiday airline tickets and as I evaluate how best to handle it, I thought I would solicit your feedback, dear readers.

We want to spend Christmas in Germany this year and arrive the weekend before Christmas. My wife’s family is having a big Christmas party the weekend before and as many of her family is aging, it’s important that we are there.

My objective, as with every transatlantic trip, is to use points to pay for the ticket, preferably in premium cabin, and even more preferably on the outbound overnight flight to Europe.

But have you checked Christmas fares from the USA to Europe lately? They are through the roof! Last year, I had no trouble getting SAS business class tickets on Christmas Eve to Europe (though from Chicago instead of Los Angeles), returning on New Year’s. This year SAS has nothing and we need to fly earlier anyway…at the same time many others are also trying to go.

Economy class tickets are pushing $2,000 each and I don’t see anything close to saver space on the usual suspects (I’m monitoring space using Atmos, AAdvantage, Aeroplan, Avios, Flying Blue, and MileagePlus, I’m also using tools like Seats.Aero to track award space).

But at this point, there’s really nothing…and I’m not being picky. I’ll take economy class or long layovers, but I’m just not willing to pay 4-5x saver pricing or the current cash price.

I can handle this is one of three ways. First, I can just wait and hope that saver space opens. It’s too early to tell how full these flights will get, but waiting for saver space to open has generally worked in the past with a couple days of flexibility.

Second, I can buy the tickets now in case the price goes up later. If book with United, if the price goes down I can cancel and rebook, baking the residual as a future flight credit. If I wait and do nothing, I may end up spending even more as well get closer to travel because this trip is happening no matter what (God willing…).

The third option would be flying to Germany a week earlier and staying a week later…the luxury of time. But that’s not ideal because I would have to pull the kids out of school (1st and 4th grade) and I’m very busy myself. My wife’s schedule would not allow it – she’s traveling on set dates regardless of cost (and yes, I’ve also been tracking single award seats for her).

I’m less worried about the kids missing school than me trying to work from Germany, which is great for blogging but not so good for the other work that I do.

Am I missing anything? Let me know your thoughts because I’ll feel a lot better once I have something booked, but I’d feel like a sucker if I ended up paying that much for coach tickets….

#6047. Awkwafina Takes Us on a Nostalgic Food-Tour of NYC's Koreatown

“It's so cool that in this city you have SoHo and Times Square but also these enclaves where you can totally belong,” says Nora Lum, the actor and comedian also known as Awkwafina. We're upstairs at the 24-hour Miss Korea, her go-to spot in Manhattan's Koreatown, picking our way over a lavish Korean barbecue spread of assorted banchan and gleaming chargrilled short ribs. “I love this!” she says, before popping a clump of braised burdock into her mouth.

Lum, who is Korean-Chinese American, has just wrapped filming Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, an unscripted Apple TV series that she hosts and executive-produces. A descendant of the family behind the legendary Cantonese American restaurant Lum's, which her great-grandfather ran in Flushing, Queens, from 1953 to 1982, she spends eight episodes gathering cooking tips from the nation's Asian communities, particularly its Chinatowns. She heads to America's oldest Chinatown, in San Francisco, to cook with chef Martin Yan, who, using “insane” knife work, “absolutely destroyed a chicken in 16 seconds”; Texas for a barbecue-fueled road trip with comedian Jimmy O. Yang, making pit stops at Korean-American-owned Eaker Barbecue in Fredericksburg and Thai-American Curry Boys BBQ in San Antonio; and Los Angeles to wait tables at the dim sum joint Golden Dragon. All these experiences lead to her own pop-up revival of Lum's in Manhattan's Little Italy, where she serves beloved staples like orange chicken and barbecue beef to friends and family.

Lum crosses 32nd Street in the heart of New York City’s Koreatown.

At its heart Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook is about heritage, community, and small-business immigrant entrepreneurship. “After the pandemic so many mom-and-pop shops were closing and Chinatowns were declining,” says Lum. “The show is about exploring that phenomenon but then also seeing who in my generation is keeping it going.”

Our first lunch stop is Miss Korea, on 32nd Street between Broadway and Fifth Avenue, the stretch where Koreatown first emerged in the late 1970s. Then home to a Korean-language bookstore and a smattering of restaurants, it's since evolved into an around-the-clock entertainment hub for anyone looking to pick up K-pop memorabilia, sing karaoke, and eat everything from Korean corn dogs at Jongro Rice Hotdog to a Michelin-starred tasting menu at Joo Ok. For Lum it's a nostalgic stretch of the city. “I went to MK, Maru, Circle,” she says in reference to nightlife spots frequented by Korean American party kids coming of age in 1990s and 2000s New York. “Oh man, I've been so messy on this one block.”

Patrons fill the tables at the ever-popular BCD Tofu House, which specializes in soondubu.

We cross the street to BCD Tofu House for crispy seafood pancakes, spicy marinated crab slicked with red pepper seasoning, and Lum's favorite: the signature soondubu, a tofu stew bubbling in a clay pot. Since opening in 2008, the Los Angeles export has increasingly drawn long lines—a testament to the growing popularity of Korean food across the US. “Twenty years ago customers were 70 to 80 percent Korean,” general manager Alex Kim tells us. “Now it's a lot more non-Korean.”

Lum notes that, for a long time in the US, immigrants selling their traditional cuisines were often met with gratitude within the culture yet distrust outside of it. Adaptation followed: the invention of chop suey, for example, and wok-fired cooking of non-Chinese vegetables like broccoli. Her great-grandfather experienced this himself with Lum's, and local appreciation for the restaurant's Americanized Chinese classics like egg rolls and shrimp with lobster sauce has remained long after it closed. “I learned to think about it less as my family's attempt at just making money but rather, ‘Hey, this is the cuisine that we ate growing up,’ ” she says. “It's a fascinating story of belonging and acculturation.”

We wander over to Woorijip, a fast-casual institution for snacking and soju drinking to pick up kimbap, and then to food hall Food Gallery 32. “This is where I get the fish!” Lum says of bungeoppang, the fish-shaped pastry introduced to Korea by Japanese colonists in the 1930s and popularized again in the '90s. In Manhattan this is the rare spot to find it.

Freshly made bungeoppang lined up at Food Gallery 32

While filming, Lum prioritized places that are moving the needle forward while still preserving their communities' culture, like Phoenix Palace in Manhattan's Chinatown. The Cantonese American restaurant hosts local elders at affordable rates and buys plates from Wing on Wo & Co., a porcelain shop dating back to 1925. Lum recalls co-owner Cory Ng's father appearing with ingredients sourced from the neighborhood.

“Chinatown is totally a local economy,” she says. But it's also where immigrants can speak their native languages, play mahjong, eat dim sum, and celebrate Lunar New Year. “So when you see Chinatowns decline, it's a bigger problem”—a problem she hopes her show can help resolve.

In San Antonio, bright pink barbecue spot Curry Boys BBQ run by three childhood friends dishes out Southeast Asian–Texan blends like oak-smoked brisket with green curry. “They're combining their own cultures into something that's so authentic to where they're from,” says Lum.

For the show, Lum waited tables at classic banquet hall Golden Dragon in Los Angeles's Chinatown, which, with its traditional dim sum service, has remained a stronghold for 64 years. Step outside, says Lum, and “it looks like a movie set.”

Lum stopped by Oahu's Kō Hana Distillers while visiting Hawaii to learn about the tiki culture that inspired her great-grandfather's drinks menu. Come here for its farm-to-bottle selection using homegrown sugarcane.

In San Francisco, the nation's oldest Chinatown “serves the community in a different way from elsewhere,” says Lum. She also loves the comparatively younger, yet still landmark, Mister Jiu's for its Western take on Cantonese cooking.

#6046. Air India CEO Wants ‘More Widebody Aircraft’

Air India is looking to buy more widebody jets as it expands overseas and works to return to profitability.

“We want more widebody aircraft,” CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said Tuesday at the Aviation India and South Asia summit in New Delhi, according to Reuters. The carrier has held talks with both Airbus and Boeing. Gebremariam did not say how many aircraft Air India might buy.

The airline’s most recent Boeing order, announced in January, was for 30 narrowbodies: 20 737 MAX 8s and 10 MAX 10s.

The carrier is also updating the widebodies it already flies. In April, Air India took delivery of the first of 26 older Boeing 787-8s slated for cabin retrofits. The aircraft went from two cabins to three with the addition of premium economy.

Gebremariam, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines, described high operating costs as a “major concern” but said he expects Air India to return to profitability “very soon.”

Air India Group lost S$3.56 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, according to financial disclosures from Singapore Airlines, which owns a 25% stake in the group. The loss came as the carrier dealt with disruption from the war in Iran and Pakistan’s closure of its airspace to Indian airlines.

#6045. American, Delta, And United Accused Of Collusion To Keep Airfares High

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and other major carriers face new lawsuits alleging they share sensitive pricing and shopping data to keep airfares higher than they would otherwise be. While watching competitors’ prices is ordinary business, pooling information in a way that discourages competition deserves a much closer look.

View From The Wing highlights two proposed class actions targeting the Airline Tariff Publishing Company (ATPCO), its subsidiary 3Victors, and major U.S. airlines.

The Washington complaint names airline companies including American, Delta, United, Southwest, Alaska, Hawaiian, and JetBlue. A separate Virginia complaint targets ATPCO, 3Victors, and a smaller group of carriers.

A central question these lawsuits raise is worth examining: does greater visibility into competitors’ pricing help airlines offer better deals, or make them less inclined to offer deals at all?

ATPCO is an airline-owned company that has long distributed fares and fare rules. The complaints challenge an expansion into pooled shopping data, alleging that participating airlines exchange commercially sensitive information through a common platform and use it to coordinate pricing.

Shopping data can reveal demand before a passenger purchases anything. Searching for a flight generates information about the itinerary requested and the offers returned, even if the customer closes the browser without booking.

On its own website, 3Victors describes participation in Iris this way:

“The more you contribute, the more you receive.”

Its PriceEye description promotes alerts and tools that identify market undercuts and overpricing. Meanwhile, DemandView promises insight into where travelers want to go before they book.

Those descriptions explain why airlines would find the products useful but they do not, at least by descriptions alone, establish that using them violates antitrust law.

The plaintiffs’ concern is that exchanging this information reduces the uncertainty that encourages airlines to compete.

Consider this example. An airline has seats to fill and thinks a lower fare could attract passengers from a competitor. Cutting the price makes sense if it can win enough additional business.

But suppose its competitors can spot and match the discount almost immediately. The airline may gain little additional business while collecting less money from passengers who would have booked anyway. That could make discounting less attractive in the first place.

But there’s a difference between that (legitimate) concern and proving that these particular arrangements unlawfully suppress competition…we’d need to see evidence about what the airlines actually exchange and how they use it.

A sophisticated pricing dashboard is not necessarily evidence of a conspiracy, for I can think of a counterexample.

If American discovers that United is charging $100 less for a comparable flight, it might lower its fare. Passengers benefit. Better information about demand could also help an airline identify an opportunity to add service.

I use comparison tools when buying tickets…I would hardly expect an airline to set its prices without looking at what competitors charge.

The harder question concerns reciprocal access to sensitive information that competitors would not otherwise possess. What exactly is being contributed? How current and detailed is it? Does the arrangement support independent decisions or weaken the incentive to compete?

My concern as a passenger is straightforward. Airlines have become very good at identifying how much we might be willing to pay. I want them to remain equally concerned that another carrier will offer us a better deal. An industry in which competitors can readily anticipate one another’s behavior deserves scrutiny, particularly when the information comes from an exchange they collectively support.

If these cases proceed into discovery, I will be interested in what the contracts and internal communications reveal…I am not ready to declare these lawsuits winners or losers, though I think View From The Wing is probably right that this airlines appear to have th stronger arguments.

Two new lawsuits allege that major U.S. airlines are using shared shopping and pricing information to weaken competition and sustain higher fares. The companies’ public product descriptions establish that extensive competitive data tools exist, though that does not prove unlawful conduct.

Better information can produce lower fares. It can also make an airline more confident that it need not offer one. I want airlines competing aggressively for my business, and these cases raise a fair question about whether their shared data arrangements encourage that competition or undermine it, a fascinating lawsuit indeed.

#6043. Six Hours Of Sleep On An Eight-Hour Flight: SAS Business Class Delivered

I mentioned earlier this week we decided to take a last-minute trip to Europe, flying in SAS A330 Business Class. This flight could not have been smoother and I’m so thankful my kids are now such excellent travelers.

We connected through Chicago and spent some time at the excellent Delta Sky Club (it’s huge!) prior to boarding. The Air France Lounge is nice, but the Delta Lounge is even nicer. Full review coming.

Lingering in the lounge, we were among the last to board, finding our seats in the center sections of row one and two.

It was evening and we were tired, but would we be able to sleep?

Dinner service commenced after takeoff and the food on SAS is excellent.

Heidi ordered the fish and I ordered the short ribs, with the intention of sharing, which is something we like doing when we fly together. That said, the salmon was fine by the beef was really delicious, as were the appetizers.

Claire Marie and Augustine did the same thing, with one having beef and the other fish and then sharing. I loved how the kids were so quiet and well-behaved, enjoyed the in-flight-entertainment and also each other’s company.

After dinner the kids went to sleep immediately and Heidi and I soon did as well. A flight attendant asked if we wanted to be awakened for breakfast and we all said no, though I asked if I could have a cappuccino at the top of descent.

We all slept very well…six hours…which is pretty amazing for a flight that is only eight hours long.

As we began our descent, a FA remembered without even my prompting to bring over the cappuccino, which was enjoyable. Heidi slept a bit longer, awaking just 20 minutes before landing. She wanted coffee and was obliged…a great crew.

I’m happy to take family trips to together, though I hope the kids are soon old enough that they can fly economy class while Heidi and I fly business class. Why? Because they can sleep in any seat and the IFE is the same in business versus premium economy or economy. That’s a whole different issue that we can discuss at some future point.

Oh, the purser had an interesting “political” pin, which I’ll discuss next week. But a great flight. Hopefully no jet lag…

They say the best deals never last forever, and in the world of points and miles, that's unquestionably true.

And after a pretty great run, one of the best deals in travel is about to get much harder to earn.

Thanks to major changes coming to Southwest Rapid Rewards in 2027, the days of using big credit card welcome bonuses to quickly earn a Southwest Companion Pass are almost over.

That's a big deal because the Companion Pass lets you bring a designated companion along on Southwest flights for just the cost of taxes and fees, starting at $5.60 each way. And you can use it again and again and again while your pass is valid.

But there's some good news if you've been hoping to earn one the quick and easy way.

You still have one last chance to use Southwest credit card welcome bonuses to help unlock a Companion Pass that's valid through the end of 2027. And the timing is especially good right now because Southwest just increased the welcome offers on its credit cards.

For example, the (see rates and fees) is currently offering 90,000 bonus points after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

That's two-thirds of the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn a Companion Pass under the current rules, just from one welcome bonus.

There's just one catch: You need to apply and be approved for an eligible Southwest credit card by Dec. 2, 2026, to take advantage of this opportunity.

Here's how to make this strategy work one last time before the rules change.

Related: Southwest Rapid Rewards: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more

To earn a Southwest Companion Pass under the current rules, you need to earn 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year. Normally, all those points would need to post to your Southwest account by Dec. 31, but Southwest is making a special exception as it transitions to its new rules for 2027.

As long as you're approved for an eligible Southwest credit card by Dec. 2, 2026, its welcome-bonus points can still count toward qualification under the 2026 Companion Pass rules, even if they post in early 2027.

That means you have a little more time to meet the spending requirement and earn those bonus points. However, you still need to earn enough qualifying points from other eligible activities in 2026.

And importantly, if you aren't approved for a Southwest credit card by Dec. 2, 2026, the welcome bonus points won't count toward a Companion Pass under this special exception.

Here's an example of how this could work.

Let's say you've already earned 45,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in 2026 from flying Southwest or using eligible partners, such as hotels, rental cars and the Rapid Rewards shopping portal.

That leaves you needing another 90,000 qualifying points to unlock the pass — that's where the newly increased Southwest credit card offers come in.

If you apply for and are approved for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Priority Credit Card by Dec. 2, and then earn its 90,000-point welcome bonus after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months, you could have enough points to earn a Southwest Companion Pass valid through Dec. 31, 2027. The everyday spending you put on the card also earns points that can help you get closer to qualifying for the pass.

And once you earn the pass, you're able to bring your designated companion along on Southwest flights as often as you want in 2027, paying just the taxes and fees.

Of course, not everyone already has around 45,000 qualifying points earned in 2026. But there's potentially another way to earn enough points before this opportunity disappears.

The timing couldn't be much better if you're hoping to earn a Southwest Companion Pass before the rules change, as Southwest just increased the welcome offers on all five of its credit cards.

Here are the current offers to consider if you want to take advantage of this opportunity before the Dec. 2 deadline.

These are limited-time offers, and we don't yet know when they will end. And remember that you need to be approved by Dec. 2, 2026, to take advantage of the special rules allowing these welcome bonuses to count toward a Companion Pass under the current qualification requirements.

The information for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Let's say you aren't on track to earn enough points to qualify for a Southwest Companion Pass one last time with just the points from one Southwest credit card bonus.

A natural question from the creative set of points enthusiasts who want to go all-in on Southwest might be ... can you get two Southwest credit card bonuses to count in one year?

The short answer is yes — in one specific situation.

Under Chase's current application restrictions, you're generally ineligible for another Southwest personal card if you already hold one, and previous welcome bonuses can also affect your eligibility.

On top of that, you must have at least 24 months between Southwest personal card welcome bonuses. So if you got one in early 2026, you can't get another now in late 2026, even if you no longer have the first card.

However, having a Southwest personal card doesn't necessarily prevent you from qualifying for a Southwest business card, though Chase's 5/24 rule can still affect your eligibility.

The rules for Southwest business cards state that you cannot currently have that particular card and you cannot have received a welcome bonus on that particular card in the past 24 months.

So, depending on your eligibility, that means you could potentially combine the welcome bonuses from a Southwest personal card and a Southwest business card to earn enough points for a Companion Pass.

For example, the currently offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months, while the offers 60,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months.

That's a combined 140,000 bonus points, enough to reach the current 135,000-point Companion Pass threshold without even counting the points earned from meeting the spending requirements.

Southwest is in the process of dramatically reshaping its airline, its loyalty program and virtually everything in between. There will be lounges, a premium credit card and a more traditionally structured elite status program where the top tier comes with a Companion Pass.

And the credit cards will certainly play a large role in that reshaped airline well into the future.

But in the midst of all that change, we are looking down the barrel of a quickly approaching 'one last time' deadline if you want to get a Southwest credit card and have the welcome bonuses help you earn a Companion Pass.

Whether you're combining a bonus with points you've already earned or considering a personal and business card strategy, the key deadline is Dec. 2, 2026. You'll need to apply and be approved by then to take advantage of the special transition rules.

If you qualify, you could earn a Companion Pass valid through Dec. 31, 2027, allowing you to bring a designated companion on eligible Southwest flights for just the cost of taxes and fees.

#6041. Can Dubai Become the World's Fittest City?

At 6 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road will fall silent. For one morning only, the city's six-lane superhighway—usually a blur of Nissan Patrols, taxis, and delivery scooters—will belong to tens of thousands of competitors as Dubai Run takes over the city’s skyline at dawn, following in the footsteps of a record 307,000 participants last year.

Leading the charge is usually Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the driving force behind the Dubai Fitness Challenge (DFC) and one of the city's most ambitious experiments: to turn itself into the fittest city in the world.

"The people of Dubai have created an inspirational fitness movement, sending a powerful message that traveled far beyond our city,” Sheikh Hamdan said during a previous edition of the challenge. “Together, let us transform Dubai into the fittest city in the world.”

An athlete himself, the Crown Prince has long championed cycling, diving, and long-distance running, but the challenge—now in its tenth year—is his most visible legacy. Launched in 2017, it calls on residents and visitors alike to commit to 30 minutes of exercise every day for 30 days each November. Since its inception, more than 16 million people have taken part, transforming what began as a simple invitation to get moving into one of the world’s largest community fitness initiatives.

This year’s landmark edition is running until Sunday, November 29 under the theme What’s Your 30x30?, inviting residents and visitors to find their own way to complete 30 minutes of daily activity. With four flagship events, three free Fitness Villages, and more than 30 Community Fitness Hubs, the program is among the most ambitious yet, transforming everything from beaches and public parks to shopping centers and major roads into places to exercise.

The first Dubai Fitness Challenge took place in 2017

Four major events headline the 2026 calendar: Dubai Ride, which opened the challenge on Sunday, November 1 with thousands of cyclists taking over Sheikh Zayed Road; Dubai Run, the world’s largest free community fun run, on Sunday, November 22; Dubai Stand-Up Paddle, a two-day festival of paddle boarding, kayaking and yoga at Hatta Dam on Saturday, November 7 and Sunday, November 8; and Dubai Yoga, which returns for its second edition on Sunday, November 29, bringing thousands together for a mass sunrise session beneath the DIFC Gate Building.

Three Fitness Villages—at Kite Beach, Zabeel Park and Al Warqa’a—act as free, all-day wellness hubs offering everything from boxing and beach volleyball to spin classes and meditation. More than 30 neighborhood Community Hubs have also been set up across the city, bringing fitness closer to home with pop-up runs, rooftop yoga, skateboarding lessons, padel tournaments, and family-friendly bootcamps.

The calendar aligns with a packed line-up of international sporting events, from the Dubai Premier Padel P1 and T100 Triathlon to the DP World Tour Championship and Emirates Dubai 7s. This year also brings the return of the Dubai Sail Grand Prix, with high-speed catamarans racing off the city’s coastline, while HYROX Dubai will see athletes tackle a grueling combination of running and functional fitness challenges. Elsewhere, the program includes obstacle races, mountain trails in Hatta, and community running events across the city.

It’s all part of what His Excellency Saeed Hareb, Secretary General of the Dubai Sports Council, describes as a lasting change in the city’s relationship with exercise. “It has helped establish a culture of active living, bringing communities together and making sport and physical activity an integral part of life in Dubai,” he said as the challenge marked its tenth anniversary.

Ahmed Al Khaja, CEO of Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment, says the anniversary is an opportunity to reflect on how far the initiative has come. Speaking at the launch of the 2026 program, he credited the collaboration between government bodies, private businesses, and local communities with making exercise increasingly accessible across Dubai. The aim, he said, is to inspire healthier habits that continue long after the 30-day challenge ends.

The numbers suggest it’s working. Last year’s edition attracted a record three million-plus participants, up from 2.73 million in 2024. More than 307,000 people took part in Dubai Run alone, while Dubai Ride welcomed 40,327 cyclists. Since the challenge launched in 2017, cumulative participation has exceeded 16 million, a remarkable figure for an initiative that began with a simple invitation to exercise for half an hour a day.

The Dubai Ride closes the city's busiest highway for one morning each year

Ethan Matthews, Chief Operating Officer at Reset Fitness and a former professional rugby player and coach in Portugal and Italy, says that Dubai’s greatest fitness asset is its variety. “There are world-class facilities on every block now—not just gyms, but parks, cycling tracks, and sports complexes,” he says. “Try as many things as possible—team sports, group sessions, individual training. It’s about finding what challenges you physically but also what you actually enjoy. That’s how you stay consistent, especially on the tough days.”

For Matthews, the social aspect is just as vital. “The moment you find something you like—padel, CrossFit, running, whatever—you meet people. It opens doors, both personally and professionally. That’s what keeps Dubai’s fitness culture alive.”

Anthony Lee, a personal trainer and owner of Activ8 Lifestyle & Fitness who has spent nearly two decades as part of Dubai’s fitness scene, thinks the timing of the challenge is part of its success. “It’s clever,” he says. “It's just before Christmas, when everyone wants to feel a bit fitter before heading home for the holidays, and when the weather’s perfect for being outdoors.”

He describes the month-long initiative as “a push that gets people back into routine,” and a rare opportunity to sample new workouts without cost or commitment. “You can try boxing on Kite Beach one day, yoga in Zabeel Park the next. It breaks the monotony.” What stands out most, he adds, is accessibility. “You don’t have to be an athlete. It’s about being a better version of yourself—you versus you.”

For visitors, the challenge offers a very different way to experience Dubai as, during November, the city’s hotels, cafes and shopping centers adopt a surprisingly sporty rhythm. At Kite Beach, sunrise yoga sessions fill up fast, while the public running track buzzes with tourists and locals alike, and Zabeel Park hosts evening workouts beneath the skyline. There's no need to sign up—just show up on the day.

Outside of November, the spirit of the challenge remains. Dubai has built more than 557 kilometers of cycle tracks, with a goal of 1,000 kilometers by 2030, and the urban planning department is adding shaded walking routes to make exercise feasible for longer stretches of the year.

Lee, the personal trainer, believes Dubai’s fitness drive has found fertile ground because of the city’s demographic and design. “It’s a young place,” he says. “Most people are working-age expats, and with the beach and pool culture here, people want to look and feel good.”

But vanity isn’t the whole story. “Every new residential tower has a gym and a pool, so exercise is built into daily life,” he says. “When I moved here 18 years ago, you had a handful of hotel gyms and a couple of Fitness First branches. Now every neighborhood has options, from boutique studios to outdoor circuits.” He has also noticed a social shift: “Fitness has become a way to meet people. For newcomers, joining a class or trying padel is how you find your tribe.”

This year’s Dubai Fitness Challenge runs under the theme What’s Your 30x30?

The fitness calendar's cleverest invention, however, might be the Mallathon. With summer temperatures soaring past 45°C, nine of the city’s biggest malls were converted into indoor running routes between June and September, attracting 100,000 participants.

Dr Amir Firouzjaei, a general practitioner and traditional Chinese medicine expert who has lived in Dubai for three years, believes the movement taps into something deeper. “When a city moves, its energy moves,” he says. “It’s not only about training the body but refreshing the mind and spirit.”

He explains that the city’s blend of high-intensity exercise and restorative practices “keeps the balance between energy and recovery,” preventing burnout and encouraging people to “stick with it.”

The trend is filtering into Dubai's hospitality scene, too. New-generation hotels such as SIRO One Za’abeel pitch themselves as “fitness and recovery” spaces, complete with in-room stretching areas, altitude chambers and performance coaches. In Al Quoz, the Matcha Club—a blend of padel courts, co-working space, and cafe—has become the new social hang-out for the health-minded. Even Dubai’s famously indulgent brunches are getting lighter, with restaurants like Eat Well dishing up bowls, turmeric shots, and cold-brew coffee instead of the traditional Champagne towers.

Matthews, who moved to Dubai in 2017—the same year the first Dubai Fitness Challenge launched—says he’s watched the city’s attitudes shift dramatically. “Post-Covid, the appetite for fitness just exploded,” he says. “Gyms, studios and open-air facilities have multiplied, but more importantly, people’s reasons for exercising have changed. They’re doing it to feel good, not just to look good.”

He believes that’s partly because of education and access. “The government has played a big role through campaigns like 30x30, but accessibility is the real game changer. Whether it’s walking paths, beach gyms or purpose-built cycling tracks, there’s always somewhere to move.” For Matthews, that accessibility underpins a healthy, sustainable economy. “When people feel better, they perform better—at work, at home, everywhere. Fitness has become part of Dubai.”

Residents and visitors alike are invited to discover new ways to move, connect and build healthy habits that last beyond the challenge's 30 days

Firouzjaei, the doctor, sees Dubai’s fitness boom as part of a wider cultural shift. “It’s a fast city, and that creates pressure,” he says. “People here work hard and compete hard, so they need ways to recharge and reset.”

He points out that the city’s international mix has made wellness more mainstream. “Residents come from everywhere—Asia, Europe, the Middle East—and many already know yoga, acupuncture, or functional medicine,” he says. “They’re open to new ideas and they understand that health is an investment rather than a luxury.” In his clinic, he’s noticed that even patients who once focused purely on appearance now talk about sleep, stress, and balance.

Behind the lifestyle messaging lies the emirate's urban agenda. Dubai wants to be a ‘20-minute city,’ where every resident can reach work, shops, and recreation within a short cycle or walk. The health argument is compelling. Obesity and diabetes are major public health concerns across the Gulf, and studies show only one in five UAE children meets recommended daily activity levels. City officials believe that building infrastructure—parks, cycle paths, open gyms—is the surest way to shift behavior.

Already, habits are changing. Park footfall has risen 20% year-on-year, while corporate wellness participation has grown by 30%. The once-novel sight of commuters jogging to metro stations has become almost ordinary.

According to experts, Dubai's mix of international residents has made wellness more mainstream

For tourists, taking part couldn’t be easier. The Dubai Fitness Challenge app lists daily events, classes, and pop-ups across the city, most of them free.

Looking back on 18 years in Dubai, Lee says the transformation has been “massive.” When he first arrived, “there were far fewer gyms, and fitness wasn’t part of daily conversation.” Now, he says, it’s as visible as the skyline itself. “Sure, some people join the big events just for the photos—you’ll always have that—but for others it’s the start of something lasting,” he says. “Even if they only do the challenge for a month, it plants a seed. And that’s what counts.”

Matthews agrees, though he cautions against seeing Dubai’s fitness scene as something reserved for the elite. “The biggest misconception is that you have to be in peak shape to take part,” he says. “You don’t. Fitness here is for everyone, from people training for Ironman to those who just want to walk their dogs or join a weekend bootcamp.”

Dubai has always been a city in motion, but now it wants its progress measured not by the height of its towers or the size of its megaprojects, but by footsteps, pedal strokes and heartbeats. It's a city that’s, quite literally, on the move—and inviting the world to keep up.

Dubai’s biggest community running event transforms Sheikh Zayed Road into a traffic-free running track, with participants choosing between a 5km route through Downtown Dubai or a longer 10km course finishing beneath the DIFC Gate Building. More than 307,000 runners took part last year.

Where: Sheikh Zayed Road, starting near the Museum of the FutureWhen: Sunday, November 22, 6.30 a.m.How to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Marking the finale of Dubai Fitness Challenge, thousands of yoga enthusiasts will gather beneath the iconic DIFC Gate Building for a mass sunrise session. The program includes guided breathwork, a sound bath and a 30-minute yoga session, with dedicated areas for families and women.

Where: DIFC Gate BuildingWhen: Sunday, November 29, sunriseHow to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Dubai’s largest beachfront Fitness Village returns with everything from spinning and yoga to padel, beach volleyball, basketball and cricket. There are dedicated activity zones, bookable courts and daily fitness classes, with the Arabian Gulf providing a rather spectacular backdrop.

Where: Kite Beach, JumeirahWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 3 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends 7 a.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Zabeel Park’s Fitness Village returns with boxing, spinning, basketball, padel, and daily group workouts, alongside dedicated children’s activities. The village also serves as the official bib collection point for Dubai Run.

Where: Zabeel Park, Gate 2When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 4 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends noon–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Set among palm trees and parkland, this neighborhood-style Fitness Village combines outdoor exercise with family-friendly activities. There’s a 2.8km running and cycling track, bike rentals, daily fitness classes, dedicated ladies-only areas and courts for padel, volleyball, football, and basketball.

Where: Al Warqa’a ParkWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; daily 4 p.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

#6040. Analysis: Airbus A350 Passengers Often Don't Feel As Tired After Flying Long-Haul Compared To A Boeing 777

George Mutch & Michael Derrer Fuchs | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Passengers stepping off a 12-hour flight may feel noticeably better after traveling on an Airbus A350 than after making a similar journey aboard an older Boeing 777. The difference is not simply a matter of seat comfort or airline service. The A350 was designed around a newer cabin environment, incorporating lower pressurization altitude, improved humidity retention, and noise-control measures intended to reduce the physical strain of spending many hours in the air.

These features have a credible scientific basis for mattering, though the evidence requires qualification. No major controlled study has directly compared passenger fatigue after equivalent A350 and 777 flights. Aircraft configuration, airline operating practices, seating density, sleep opportunity, and individual health all influence how travelers feel. Nevertheless, the A350 offers several potential advantages over many earlier 777s, particularly on very long sectors. Those benefits can make the journey less taxing, even though they cannot eliminate jet lag.

One of the A350's most consequential comfort features is its ability to maintain a lower cabin altitude. Although the aircraft may cruise above 35,000 feet, its pressurization system keeps the cabin environment at a much lower equivalent altitude. Airbus specifies a cabin altitude of 6,000 feet (1,828 meters) for the A350, a level made possible in part by its carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic fuselage. Older Boeing 777 variants generally operate within the conventional commercial-aircraft limit of 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) at maximum operating altitude. This is a regulatory ceiling, not a guarantee that every 777 flight remains at precisely 8,000 feet. Actual cabin altitude changes during a flight and varies with operating conditions. Even so, the potential difference between a 6,000-foot A350 cabin and an 8,000-foot cabin is physiologically meaningful.

A 2007 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine examined 502 volunteers during simulated flights in a controlled hypobaric chamber. Researchers exposed participants to cabin pressures equivalent to altitudes ranging from 650 feet to 8,000 feet. At the highest simulated altitude, average oxygen saturation fell by as much as 4.4 percentage points compared with the lowest condition. Participants also reported more discomfort, including fatigue and muscular discomfort, at 7,000 to 8,000 feet. Those differences emerged after three to nine hours of exposure.

The researchers did not find that the lower oxygen levels caused acute mountain sickness or measurable impairment in sensory and psychomotor testing. Their conclusion was more specific: maintaining a cabin altitude of 6,000 feet or lower could reduce passenger discomfort on long flights. This supports the A350's approach, but it does not prove that every traveler will arrive less tired or that the aircraft prevents fatigue. Pressurization performance varies by generation and operating conditions. Nevertheless, the A350's lower target gives it a tangible advantage in an area where scientific research has established a relationship between cabin altitude and passenger discomfort.

Cabin humidity is another factor that can influence how comfortable passengers feel after a long flight. The air supplied to aircraft cabins at cruising altitude is extremely dry. Relative humidity on many long-haul flights commonly falls between 10% and 20%, well below levels people experience indoors on the ground. Low humidity does not normally cause clinically significant dehydration in healthy passengers. It can, however, dry the eyes, nose, throat, and skin, making a long journey feel less comfortable. Increasing cabin humidity improved nasal comfort while reducing ocular, nasal, and skin symptoms.

The A350's composite fuselage helps address an engineering constraint behind cabin humidity. Traditional aluminum structures are more vulnerable to corrosion when exposed to sustained moisture, so aircraft manufacturers have historically limited humidity to reduce the risk of condensation and structural deterioration. Composite materials are less susceptible to that form of corrosion, giving designers greater flexibility to manage moisture levels.

Airbus says the A350 combines its carbon-fiber structure with improved humidity levels during cruise, contributing to lower passenger fatigue. Independent aviation-health research also notes that newer composite aircraft, including the A350 and Boeing 787, can retain more moisture than older designs. Cruise humidity around 15% has been reported in some cases. This does not mean every A350 cabin remains at 15% to 20% throughout a flight. Humidity varies with passenger numbers, ventilation rates, and operating conditions, and it is not routinely monitored in commercial cabins. Passengers may notice fewer dry-eye symptoms or less irritation after many hours, particularly when improved moisture retention accompanies lower cabin altitude. Humidity alone is unlikely to determine whether someone arrives exhausted, but it can remove one source of discomfort that becomes more noticeable as flight time increases.

The A350's reputation as a 'passenger favorite' masks a more complex truth for flight crews, whose rest experiences can vary widely.

Noise is less straightforward to compare because measurements depend on where they are taken, which engines power the aircraft, the phase of flight, and the seating area. Airbus describes the A350 as the quietest aircraft in its category and says its noise-optimized airframe and engine nacelles can make it up to nine decibels quieter than competing aircraft. The Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines, aerodynamic design, and cabin insulation contribute to its acoustic environment.

Independent measurements offer a more restrained picture. Researchers found that the differences between the several widebody aircraft measured were relatively small, within approximately three decibels. The A350 was not the quietest aircraft in that particular sample, with the Airbus A380 recording the lowest levels. These findings show why manufacturer comparisons should not be interpreted as a universal passenger experience. Even small reductions in background noise can help on a long flight. A steadier acoustic environment may make it easier to read, relax, or sleep, especially for passengers sensitive to engine noise or cabin activity. Noise also interacts with other conditions: someone in a quiet business-class suite may rest better than a traveler seated near a galley, regardless of aircraft type.

The A350's cabin environment does not make it superior in every aspect of passenger comfort. The 777 has a slightly wider fuselage. That extra space can matter, especially in economy class, where airlines decide how to divide the cabin among seats, aisles, and sidewalls. Seat width depends heavily on the carrier's layout, as the 777 can be configured with nine seats across in economy or with ten seats across. The same principle applies to the A350, where a common ten-abreast economy arrangement can reduce individual seat width. Overall, aircraft dimensions therefore do not tell passengers exactly how much personal space they will receive.

Singapore Airlines provides a useful illustration of how the comparison changes by cabin. Its 777-300ER economy layout can offer wider seats than its A350-900, making the larger Boeing a potentially better choice for travelers who prioritize shoulder room. Yet the A350 may be preferable for passengers who value a lower cabin altitude, a more modern acoustic environment, and potentially less dryness on long sectors. The airline's actual seat map and aircraft assignment matter more than a simple manufacturer-versus-manufacturer ranking.

Discover five A350 features that make it feel quieter and more comfortable than Boeing's 787 on long-haul flights.

The aircraft provides the physical environment, but airlines determine many of the conditions passengers experience within it. Cabin temperature, lighting schedules, meal timing, service interruptions, seating density, and crew procedures can all influence rest. An A350 operated with bright cabin lighting during intended sleep hours or frequent service interruptions may offer less restorative rest than a carefully managed 777 flight. Passenger circumstances, including sleep before travel, departure time, stress, and seat location, also shape how travelers feel on arrival. Someone seated beside a busy galley may experience more disruption than a passenger in a quieter window seat.

For travelers choosing between comparable flights, the A350 may provide a more favorable environment for a long journey. However, aircraft substitutions and differences in airline configurations make it worth checking the scheduled aircraft and seat map before departure. It is also necessary to distinguish general travel fatigue from jet lag, which occurs when the body's internal clock falls out of alignment with local time after crossing time zones.

The A350's advantage over older 777s may also become less pronounced as Boeing introduces the 777X. The forthcoming aircraft family is being designed with a quieter cabin, improved humidity, cleaner air, and other passenger-focused upgrades. However, Boeing's often-cited 6,000-foot cabin altitude figure currently applies to its BBJ 777X business-jet offering at maximum cruise altitude. It should not automatically be treated as the confirmed specification for every future commercial 777X configuration.

Ultimately, passengers may arrive feeling less tired after flying on an A350 than on an older 777, particularly when flights are similar in duration, schedule, and cabin class. The strongest evidence concerns cabin altitude: controlled research links exposure to 7,000- and 8,000-foot cabin conditions with greater reported discomfort over time. The A350's 6,000-foot cabin target gives it a credible physiological advantage, while improved humidity and noise control can further enhance the experience. However, no evidence establishes a universal fatigue difference between the two aircraft. As the 777X introduces newer cabin technologies, the comparison will increasingly depend on aircraft generation and airline execution. Manufacturers will need to make cabin comfort more consistent if they want passengers to experience a reliably better arrival.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6039. Frontier Hires A Wizz Air Executive As Two Leaders Walk Out

Frontier announced Monday that Michael Delehant will join as Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer (COO) on November 30, 2026 according to AirlineGeeks. He most recently ran operational and commercial activities as a group Managing Director at Wizz Air, and before that he was chief strategy and network officer at Vueling; he also held several leadership roles at Southwest. He will report to Frontier CEO, Jimmy Dempsey.

The other half of the announcement is the exits. Trevor Stedke, Senior Vice President of Operations, and Alex Clerc, Senior Vice President of Customers, will both depart on November 13. Frontier didn’t provide a reason for either. Not all departures have a “spending more time with my family” boilerplate announcement provided and there’s nothing wrong with that. But  it’s telling that the person running operations and the person in charge of customers are both gone, unironically about two weeks before a new operations boss shows up for work.

James Fenner, who has spent more than a decade at Frontier and was most recently Vice president of Revenue and Loyalty, becomes Senior Vice President and Chief Revenue Officer. His job now covers pricing, revenue management, loyalty and network planning. Most of those make sense to me together with the exception of loyalty. Pricing and revenue management go hand-in-hand as does network planning. But with the Frontier getting a dedicated first class, and the loss of Spirit (so far), Allegiant/Sun Country merging, and the struggles JetBlue is facing and Frontier’s own revenue challenges – it feels like loyalty should be its own gig.

Bobby Schroeter becomes Chief Marketing Officer, overseeing the brand and customer experience. With the customers executive leaving, customer experience moves under marketing. I would have thought loyalty responsibilities would have fallen to CMO but I am apparently mistaken.

Frontier lost $104 million in the Q3 2026, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Removing special items and the airline made $40 million on a record $1.36 billion in revenue. Matthew covered it the day the numbers dropped as a loss despite record revenue, and he found reason for optimism.

Dempsey took over after longtime chief, Barry Biffle, left suddenly in December last year and was named CEO in January. This CEO, on the job about 10 months, is swapping out the operations chief, the customer chief and handing the revenue chief and in essence reinventing the carrier. I want to applaud Dempsey for taking his time to evaluate before making such dramatic changes. Newly installed leaders often want their own people and to break from the past to do things their way and make their own mark. However, as long as it has taken to make these changes, many might have presumed that he felt he was able to make those changes with the current staff in place.

Hiring a Wizz Air executive indicates what Frontier thinks its future playbook is. Delehant comes from two low-cost European carriers, Wizz and Vueling, and those two airlines operate differently from each other and the market is different from Frontier. Vueling is owned by International Airlines Group, the same parent as British Airways, Iberia, LEVEL, and Aer Lingus. Vueling operates outside of the network carrier model with connections and oneworld partner feed but still benefits from the incredible buying power of IAG. Wizz does not.

But for those who have called the death of LCCs and ULCCs in the United States with the shut down of Spirit, the new Frontier could fly in the face of that. Further, as pointed out on this site before, based solely on flying people and things, Ryan Air might be the most profitable true airline (not loyalty program) in the world. It closed last year earning $2.4bn, and every carrier that placed above Ryan had a loyalty program and credit card tie-in.

One thing that has become very clear, is that first class in the United States simply must be offered to be successful. Frontier, Allegiant/Sun Country, and JetBlue have all added a first class product this year (JetBlue had Mint for long haul but its shorter haul domestic first class is genuinely new.) Spirit had just moved into this space too, separating its Big Front Seat product into a First Class cabin, then European-style Business Class (blocked middle seat) though the writing was already on the wall in Fort Lauderdale.

These changes at Frontier could foretell the future of the ultra low cost model in the United States, first class and all.

Whether Delehunt’s changes have the capability of increasing Frontier Airlines stock price will likely determine just how much further he goes. But he’s right to install his own leadership, and given the market segment, quite savvy to find executives with experience in the ULCC space and at least some overlap in the United States in Southwest Airlines. Frontier has a credit card, its loyalty division now shares a boss with revenue management, and a hub model at least in part so it’s not a like-for-like fit with Wizz or other ULCC models. But it’s not a miss either, and I am interested in seeing just how much of the Spirit vacuum Frontier chooses to operate.

#6038. Qatar Launches Two South American Destinations

Qatar Airways added two South American destinations on Wednesday, becoming the first Gulf carrier to serve Venezuela.

The new service flies from Doha to Bogotá, Colombia, then continues to Caracas, Venezuela, before returning nonstop to Doha. Qatar Airways will operate the route on Wednesdays and Sundays using a Boeing 777-200LR.

Flights are scheduled to leave Doha at 7:35 a.m. and reach Bogotá at 4:25 p.m. After a 90-minute stop, the aircraft continues to Caracas, arriving at 9 p.m. The return flight leaves Caracas at 11:30 p.m. and reaches Doha at 8:35 p.m. the following day. All times are local.

The airline originally planned to start flying the route in July but postponed the launch following an earthquake in Venezuela, according to Aviation Week.

Qatar Airways is also expanding its codeshare with LATAM to include domestic flights from Bogotá. The agreement will put Qatar’s code on LATAM flights to destinations including Medellín, Cartagena and Cali.

The additions bring Qatar Airways’ network in the Americas to 17 destinations. The carrier began serving South America in 2010 with flights to São Paulo.

#6036. Hilton Is Growing Faster Than Marriott, Hyatt And IHG

Hilton opened 182 hotels and 27,000 rooms in the Q3 2026, which works out to 23,000 net additional rooms and net unit growth of 6% from a year prior, according to its earnings release. Net income was $536MM, up from $421MM, and adjusted EBITDA was $1.058bn. Management and franchise fee revenue rose 9.5% which is the company’s core business model.

Comparing that to the other three big loyalty hotel companies, Marriott added roughly 20,000 net rooms and grew 4.6%. IHG reported net system growth of 4.9% after opening 12,900 rooms across 92 hotels. Hyatt posted net rooms growth of 3.8% over the trailing 12 months. The companies define growth a little differently, but Hilton leads on every version I can find, and it did so while adding more net rooms in a quarter than Marriott, the larger of the two companies.

More rooms does not necessarily mean higher earnings. Hyatt’s comparable system-wide RevPAR rose 7.2%, Marriott’s rose 6.5% worldwide and 7.4% in the US and Canada, while Hilton’s rose 5.8%, and IHG’s rose just 5.3%. Hilton ranks third of four on that list which starts to eat into its net rooms added lead. Hyatt’s caveat is its all-inclusive business, where Net Package RevPAR fell 2.5%, which matters because every big hotel brand wants your all-inclusive money right now. This, for me, probably deserves its own post if the drops continue into the fourth quarter compared with YoY.

Net profit confirms the rate growth relative to both peers and net rooms is more tied to RevPAR than absolute growth. Marriott earned $794MM in the quarter and $1.52bn in adjusted EBITDA, well ahead of Hilton. Hyatt’s net income was $58MM, or $122MM adjusted, which is considerably less but HYatt is far smaller (and underperforms.) I wrote last week that Royal Caribbean out-earned Hilton’s whole 2025 in a quarter, and the hotel sector is a reminder that growth and earnings are different races.

Marriott’s development pipeline hit a record of more than 634,000 rooms across over 4,200 properties, with 44% of those rooms under construction. Hilton’s pipeline is 543,100 rooms across 3,869 hotels in 135 countries, with nearly half under construction and more than half outside the United States. IHG’s pipeline is 353,000 rooms, up 3.2% and equal to 33% of its current system. Hyatt’s is about 158,000 rooms, up 12.1%.

Marriott has the biggest pipeline in absolute terms, Hyatt’s is growing fastest of the three that disclosed growth, and Hilton grew 5%. Conversions matter here too. Marriott said conversions (existing independent hotels or those being reflagged) made up over a third of signings and over 40% of openings in the first nine months, and IHG says development splits roughly evenly between new builds and conversions. Hilton opened its first Select by Hilton hotels this quarter, one of several newer brands it is leaning on to fill that pipeline.

As someone whose agency sells hotel rooms, both of these numbers are important but for different reasons. My clients and I prefer to see the rate creep slow or stop (rate regression might be a dream) with more stays. But more properties to choose from is good news too and increases competition.

For travelers, the bigger question is what all this growth does to loyalty programs especially when comparing Hilton vs Marriott. Marriott Bonvoy and Hilton Honors each span well over a million rooms, and their luxury brands include Waldorf Astoria, Conrad, St. Regis, Ritz-Carlton and JW Marriott. But with so many of the new rooms being conversions and limited-service hotels where elite status buys less, that can reduce the shine of the programs. Lounge access and complimentary breakfast (a daily food and beverage credit at most U.S. Hilton hotels) are what business travelers chase but lounges are almost gone completely, and those perks are thinner at a select-service property. Hilton offers elites a fifth night free on standard reward stays and waives resort fees on free nights, and Hilton points pile up quickly through its brand credit cards with American Express. Long term, more hotels should mean more places to redeem, not just more places to earn. But the question also becomes how important those advantages are, and with both Bonvoy’s accelerated status earning, and Hilton’s Diamond via credit card option, the true value of those benefits continue to diminish.

Hilton returned $879MM to shareholders in the quarter, $2.9bn so far this year, and projects about $3.5 billion for 2026. It also moved its stock listing to Nasdaq on November 5, 2026 under the same HLT ticker. IHG has completed $707MM of a $950MM buyback and expects to return over $1.2bn in 2026. Hyatt projects $375MM to $425MM in capital returns. Hotels are on a tear over the last couple of years and Hilton’s growth in room count demonstrates confidence in the market for the future.

Hilton is winning the room race and not the rate race, and Marriott is winning the profit race. I expect Hilton to hold the unit growth lead through 2027, but Marriott’s larger pipeline will make that lead uncomfortable. Hyatt will continue winning on rate while sitting out the growth sprint barring another acquisition which it has been drawn to as of late, which is exactly how a luxury-leaning brand should behave. Still, it’s impressive to see Hilton with such strong numbers for growing the brand.
