#6035. 11 Gorgeous US Ski Vacation Homes Built for Fresh Powder and Easy Slope Access

I’ve been skiing my entire life, venturing out for nostalgic winter weekends on the East Coast and fresh powder-chasing adventures out West. Yet somehow, the anticipation of a new ski season never gets old. Like clockwork, every winter brings a new mountain to explore, a favorite run to revisit, and plenty of reasons to start dreaming about the next snowfall. With El Niño in the conversation and ski resorts across the US gearing up for opening day, there’s no better time to get your winter plans in order.

After all, a memorable ski vacation isn’t just about finding the right mountain (though I take my terrain very seriously). It’s also about the cozy ski towns, the lively après-ski scenes, the snow-covered scenery, and of course, the splendid place to retreat to when it’s time for boots to come off. When it comes to the best ski vacation homes, there are some amenities that really do take these trips to the next level: a hot tub to soothe your muscles, an in-unit washer and dryer to freshen up base layers, a nice fireplace or firepit to cozy up around, and a kitchen for easy meals at home—especially ideal after working up a big appetite on the mountain.

Some of the best ski vacation rentals in the US are every bit as enticing as the mountains themselves. Think glass-walled chalets, design-forward A-frames, and tucked-away cabins with easy access to the lifts. From New England favorites to Western powder havens, these 11 standout stays are worth building your next ski or snowboard getaway around.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, cedar barrel sauna, pool and ping-pong tables, arcade games, boot warmers

If you’re an avid East Coast skier, you’re likely no stranger to Killington’s buzzy ski resort, home to over 200 ski trails of terrain for any level shredder. This five-bedroom cabin makes a great launchpad for those staying in the area. The amenity-filled gem sits only four minutes away from Killington Resort, and comes with a game room, cedar barrel sauna, and mountain views for days. Use the boot warmers in the closet before hitting the mountain, then leave all your gear in the ski shed for storage once you’ve returned. In the evenings, fire up some food on the patio grill then cozy up around the wood-burning fireplace.

Where to ski: Killington Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: Killington Skyeship Base Lodge, The Lookout Tavern, Killington Village, Gifford Woods State Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows, mountain views, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

I’m adding this Vermont gem to my ski bucket list for a dozen different reasons, starting with the fact that the mountain access is second to none: This spruced-up, slopeside penthouse apartment sits steps from the ski lifts, less than just a five-minute walk to Stowe Mountain Resort’s six-passenger Over Easy Gondola. It’s also a 15-minute drive to one of my favorite mountains, Smugglers’ Notch, where the vibes are always high and the terrain is suitable for all kinds of skiers.

Back at “home,” this modern mountain aesthetic will refresh you after a long day on the slopes. A picture-perfect gas fireplace hangs in front of floor-to-ceiling windows that provide mountain views for days. Tasteful pops of color complete the dining space, comfy blankets line the couch, and the small-but-mighty kitchen has all the appliances you might need for cooking dinner.

Where to ski: Stowe Mountain Resort or Smugglers’ NotchThings to do nearby: Stowe Village, Matterhorn, Cliff House Restaurant, Gondola Skyride (to Mount Mansfield’s peak), The Club at Spruce Peak

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, wraparound deck, dining area with grill, mountain views, wood-burning fireplace

Perched 60 feet above New York’s buzzy Hunter Mountain, with a ski (or hiking) trail just across the street, this rental is ideal for a fun-filled New York ski trip not far from the city. In true log cabin fashion, guests can admire the vaulted ceiling made of cedarwood beams, indoor fireplace, and mountain-facing sliding doors which open to a wraparound deck with a firepit. There are odes to nature everywhere, from framed landscape paintings to horns and antlers as wall decor.

The home’s slopeside location is the real draw: As one previous guest wrote in an Airbnb review, “you’ll feel like you’ll have your own backdoor to Hunter Mountain.” While it’s not a true ski-in/ski-out property, the home sits a quick drive or walk away from the Hunter North area, where you can gear up and take off.

Where to ski: Hunter Mountain Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Tannersville, Hunter Mountain Brewery, Ze Burger Wine Bar, Fellow Mountain Cafe

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedroom, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: California king bed, laundry facilities, wood-burning fireplace, patio with private hot tub

This extra-luxurious abode has the look and feel of an upscale hotel—à la The Cloudveil—but it’s actually a private townhouse at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort with three bedrooms that sleep up to seven. While the prime location may be one of the biggest selling points, the decor and design make it even more enticing: The living room, for example, has classic Jackson Hole touches (note the antler chandelier and cozy fireplace), balanced out by light linens and airy textures. You might be hard-pressed to leave this homey adobe, but if and when you do decide to venture out, you can enjoy the two hot tubs and pool at the nearby Sundance Tennis and Swim Club.

Where to ski: Jackson Hole Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: JH Sports (for gear rentals), Teton Village, Moose Creek Quad Chair, Mangy Moose Jackson Hole

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, wood-burning sauna, gas grill, indoor fireplace, kid-friendly amenities, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

Where to ski: Breckenridge Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Hoosier Pass, Peaceful Valley Lodge, Downtown Breckenridge, Boreas Mountain, Quandary Peak, BreckConnect Gondola

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Fully equipped kitchen, mountain views, hot tub, firepit, central location

This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, Montana, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. And Big Sky Resort sits at the top of many Montana itineraries for good reason—especially come wintertime. Ski days here mean inviting terrain of wide-open slopes, steep chutes, and picture-perfect runs beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak. Just 10 minutes from the resort itself, this gorgeous mountain home sits on a sprawling 23 acres of land in the Lower Beehive Basin neighborhood—a backcountry ski destination in and of itself.

Inside the home, you’ll find modern cowboy country design and swanky amenities in the places that matter. For one, each of the two bedrooms feature king beds with mattress warmers to keep you cozy during winter nights. Take advantage of the big patio space for stargazing, relaxing in the hot tub, and cooking up some s’mores before heading inside for a movie night. The house can technically host up to eight guests, but it’s more ideal for families or smaller groups. Aside from the two bedrooms, the living room offers one sofa bed and two bunk beds.

Where to ski: Big Sky ResortThings to do nearby: Lone Mountain Ranch, Gallatin Peak, Big Sky Mountain Village, Fan Mountain, Beehive Peak, Madison Base (at Big Sky Resort)

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski out access, hot tub, indoor fireplace, fully equipped kitchen

When it comes to access to Utah’s renowned slopes and cool ski towns, you can’t get much better than this four-bedroom luxury penthouse. At the base of Park City Mountain, this condo boasts ski-in/ski-out access directly from the mountain's Silver Star lift. Spacious living areas, a chef’s kitchen, a hot tub, and a balcony overlooking the golf course and icy lakes create a refined on-mountain experience. The penthouse’s proximity to both ski runs and downtown makes for a seamless mix—not to mention you’ll be just a 10-minute drive to Deer Valley Resort, accessible from the condo via a free ski shuttle. With bunk beds for families and plenty of lounge areas for après-ski downtime, this Park City gem accommodates groups seeking easy access to slopes in style.

Where to ski: Park City Mountain; Deer Valley ResortThings to do nearby: Kimball Art Center, Old Town Main Street, Creekside Park, Iron Mountain Trailhead, Thaynes Canyon

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, firepit, fully equipped kitchen, game area, in-unit washer and dryer

New Mexico ski trips mean a real change of scenery, and this year there’s an extra reason to have this underrated mountain range on your radar. The state is one of the southern mountain regions set to see a spike in snowfall this winter thanks to El Niño. Lucky for those who book this cabin, you’ll be just 23 miles from Taos Ski Valley, and practically at the front door of Angel Fire Resort, a hidden gem famous for wide, smooth, groomed cruiser runs and gentler slopes. (It’s a great one for beginners, featuring the renowned Heading Home 3.2-mile green run that traverses all the way from the summit to the base.)

This home is only around 100 yards away from that exact ski run, with slope access right out the door. Inside, there’s a ton of space to sprawl out and indulge in simple creature comforts: soaking in the hot tub, roasting marshmallows around the firepit on the expansive deck, and playing board games (or one of the vintage arcade games inside the den).

Where to ski: Angel Fire Resort; Taos Ski ValleyThings to do nearby: Oeste Vista Trail, Summit Haus, Cabin at Southwest Flyer Lift, Liberation Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Wraparound deck, sauna, firepit, unique design, opt-in grocery delivery, Koyo massage chair

Mammoth is another mountain with an El Niño forecast worth keeping an eye on. Rising to 11,053 feet, the Eastern Sierra resort boasts California’s highest ski-resort summit and 3,500 acres of terrain, with plenty of room for everyone from first-timers finding their ski legs to seasoned riders chasing steeper lines. This unique mountain home near the base of the mountain takes its design cues from Japanese ryokans the host has frequented, with a soaring ceiling, dramatic dome-shaped window framing the surrounding peaks, and a loft-like den. The amenities are equally enticing: a hot tub, sauna, massage chair, optional tatami-and-futon sleeping quarters, yukatas, and an enormous shower room. Locationwise, it’s hard to beat: Canyon Lodge is less than half a mile away and walkable, while the Village and Eagle Lodge are both under a mile from the house. On especially snowy days, you may even be able to ski right down the hill and back home.

Where to ski: Mammoth Mountain Ski AreaThings to do nearby: Twin Lakes Vista, Mammoth Creek Park, Sherwin Lakes Trailhead, Mammoth Brewing Company, Canyon Lodge, Whitmore Hot Springs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside and central location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

Where to ski: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort; Aspen Snowmass Ski Resort; Aspen Highlands Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s iconically named Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s wildlife spotting in general.

It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to book elsewhere. A big plus? Big Sky’s tiny but endearing town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Where to ski: Big Sky Ski ResortThings to do nearby Lone Mountain Ranch, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center, Gondola Mid Station, Montana Jack, Beehive Basin Trailhead

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Epic Pass?

The Epic Pass offers skiing and snowboarding at a sprawling collection of USresorts. Major destinations include Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Crested Butte, Park City, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, Stevens Pass, and Stowe. There are also regional and partner resorts with more limited access, so check the specific pass tier before booking a trip. Do note that blackout dates and access limits vary by pass, so read the fine print!

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Ikon Pass?

The Ikon Pass has a tempting lineup as well, especially if your winter plans involve chasing snow across the Rockies and Sierras. Its US destinations include Mammoth Mountain, Palisades Tahoe, Steamboat, Winter Park, Aspen Snowmass, Copper Mountain, Big Sky, Jackson Hole, Taos Ski Valley, Deer Valley, Alta, Snowbird, and Sun Valley. Out east, you can head to Killington, Sugarbush, Stratton, Loon Mountain, Sugarloaf, or Sunday River.

Where is El Niño predicted to bring snowfall this season?

For the 2026-27 season, a strong El Niño is shaping the forecast, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expecting wetter-than-average conditions across the southern US, from California and the Southwest through the Southeast, as well as along the East Coast. This could mean more opportunities for snowfall in higher-elevation ski destinations, particularly when temperatures cooperate.

However, wetter doesn't automatically mean snowier: NOAA also expects warmer-than-average conditions across much of the West and northern US Seasonal outlooks predict precipitation patterns, not specific snowfall totals, so keep an eye on shorter-range forecasts before planning a powder chase.

Read more about how El Niño is impacting ski resorts here.

#6034. The Aircraft Replacing The Chinook

As it stands, there is technically no official replacement for the Boeing CH-47 yet under US Army development. Significant progress on the Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk’s successor has taken place in recent years, however. That is the Bell V-280 Valor, a tiltrotor under development that has key differences from its older cousin, Bell-Boeing’s V-22 Osprey.

The lack of a direct successor for the heavy-duty whirlybird has led to some speculation that the Army may consolidate its fleet, with the backbone model being the Valor (officially designated MV-25). Concerns about the CH-47F’s survivability in contested airspace and vast domains like the Pacific lend credence to the possibility of a total phase-out.

The Chinook’s unrivaled heavy-lift capability and outstanding track record make it a favorite with the special forces communities of the US Department of Defense. The Army’s Chinook fleet numbers more than 470 aircraft and is expected to serve as the primary heavy-lift rotorcraft for many more years to come.

Since debuting in 1961, the Chinook has never been toppled as the apex of tandem-rotor helicopters. The soviets experimented with tandem-rotor designs, but favored different configurations for heavy lift. Even the US Navy and Marines’ CH-46 has been retired for a decade. The Chinook is still being modernized, as the Block II variant offers a gross weight increase of 54,000 pounds, upgraded fuel systems, and rotor blades.

Honeywell has developed the new T55-714C, with 20% more power and 8% better fuel efficiency than previous powerplants. Vertical Mag quoted General John Murray in 2021, saying that no replacement had been planned yet, and the Chinook remains a critical asset for Army Special Forces, among other missions:

“The Future Attack Reconnaissance Aircraft and the Future Long Range Assault Aircraft are the two plans, programs we have working right now. There is nothing working for a replacement for the CH-47.”

The first CH-47F Block II Chinooks reached the Army in 2024, and the first of a scheduled 465 helicopters was delivered in July of that year, according to World of Aviation. Some compare the CH-47 to the equally enduring B-52, for being so good at what it does that there simply is no replacement. Perhaps it will soldier on into the distant future, but let's explore the latest challenger and if it has what it takes to fill the Chinooks’ place on the flightline.

The Army’s Future Vertical Lift program sought to develop the Future Long Range Assault Attack, or FLRAA. The winning platform was Bell Textron’s V-280 Valor tiltrotor. The new aircraft will initially supplement the UH-60 Black Hawk fleet but will likely replace the aging Sikorsky completely over time.

Although the V-280 is cut from the same cloth as the Bell-Boeing Osprey, engineers have implemented key differences from the start. Aside from a smaller overall footprint, the V-280 uses a V-tail configuration rather than the V-22’s twin vertical fin tail. While the V-22’s nacelles, which house both the engine and gearbox, fully rotate, only the V-280’s props and gearbox move while the engines remain fixed during transition between flight modes.

The V-280 also features a different clutch to the V-22’s problematic design, as it operates more like a conventional helicopter. The Osprey’s transmission has been linked to fatal hard-clutch engagements on more than one occasion and requires somewhere in the ballpark of 45 days to replace, according to Military.com.

The Bell V-280 Valor is a next-generation tiltrotor aircraft developed specifically by Bell-Textron for the US Army's FLRAA program. The V-280's defining feature is its ability to transition between helicopter-like vertical flight and airplane-like forward flight by tilting its rotors and drive shafts. It offers significant improvements in speed, range, and maneuverability over the UH-60.

This allows vertical takeoff and landing like a helicopter while providing speed and range comparable to a fixed-wing aircraft. Flying as fast as 300 knots, the Valor is almost twice as fast as the Chinook, which tops out at 170 knots. The Valor also surpasses the Chinook in range by a long shot.

Under combat load, the CH-47 can only go about 400 NM, while the V-280 can fly 800 NM on a single fill-up without any aerial refueling. The Valor can perform fast-rope sling-loading like the UH-60 or CH-47, but armament has yet to be publicly revealed. A key area where it falls short of the CH-47 is, inevitably, raw payload.

The V-280, or MV-25 as it recently became designated, has under half the sling-load capacity at 10,000 lbs compared to the Chinook’s 26,000 lbs. The Valor can’t compete with the Chinook in weight or volume capacity, which is the crux of the issue when it comes to replacing the venerable CH-47.

Like its Bell-Boeing V-22 Osprey predecessor, Valor’s tiltrotor design is a radical departure from conventional rotorcraft. The MV-25 is equipped with two Rolls-Royce AE 1107F engines, which are of the same powerplant family as used in the C-130 Hercules, Global Hawk drone, and V-22 Osprey.

The V-280 gearbox design has been refined from the V-22's design into a simpler, lighter, and more easily maintainable design. This new system eliminates the need for a mid-wing gearbox, which cuts the total number of gearboxes from five to four, versus the Osprey.

2,100 nautical miles (2,400 mi; 3,900 km)

The design allows for a straight wing design that reduces complexity and eliminates a number of failure points. The V-280's stationary engines result in weight savings, thanks to fewer parts, and the lower empty weight also allows for better performance and fuel efficiency.

Its simplified mechanical system also improves reliability and maintenance, reducing the notoriously long downtime seen with the Osprey as well as operational costs overall. The Valor is superior to the Chinook in the area of efficiency, and likely around the same level of complexity. Still, the question of operation costs and maintenance intensity remains unclear.

The MV-25 has the potential to revolutionize US military operations, particularly in the Pacific. There, its speed, range, and survivability are greatly superior to the CH-47 in long-range air assault missions. Its ability to take off and land vertically like a helicopter and transition to airplane-like flight profiles allows for rapid deployment and maneuverability that the Chinook can’t match in the vast, island-dotted Pacific.

This would be particularly important in any potential conflict with China. Here, long distances and limited infrastructure are major challenges for any conventional rotorcraft. The Valor greatly exceeds the capabilities of the Black Hawk in this scenario. It will enable the Army to project power across greater distances in the Pacific, like the South China Sea, more quickly and efficiently.

The MV-25 can operate from austere locations like its predecessors, and its long range can overcome logistical challenges in the vast and dispersed island chains of the Pacific. Improved survivability features make it more difficult for adversaries to target. The primary strength is speed, but it also features radar cross-section reduction and infrared suppression to minimize its detectability.

In potential conflicts with near-peer adversaries with advanced air defenses, the Valor will significantly improve the survivability of air assault operations. That also allows for more dispersed and decentralized operations over extended distances. That adaptability and flexibility make it a well-suited platform for the Pacific theater.

The US Army is undergoing a significant transformation in its aviation branch as a whole. The future will prioritize unmanned systems and more long-range crewed platforms. The Valor is one of the top priorities, as it will replace the Black Hawk, which is the current backbone of Army Aviation. The Army is also investing in long-range precision munitions for its aircraft to match its tactics to faster platforms.

The Army is rapidly working toward affordable, reliable, and lethal uncrewed aerial systems in the field. Deploying drone swarms or executing pinpoint strikes from units integrated with drones at the brigade level will evolve the Army’s strategy to the next level. The 'Replicator' initiative, headed by the Defense Innovation Unit, aims to field thousands of low-cost, autonomous systems.

The new devices would be attritable drones that counter adversary threats as well as provide man-portable intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance with strike capability. In a future of drones at the tip of the spear and tiltrotor workhorses as the backbone of the vertical lift fleet, it's hard to say if the CH-47 will still have a place.

Its raw payload-carrying power has no equal in current or planned platforms, which may see it live on in a way the B-52 has endured. On the other hand, it may simply be unneeded, as tiltrotor technology improves and other aircraft like the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency Liberty Lifter are introduced.

#6033. My Abysmal Enterprise Car Rental Experience In Omaha

Attending to a personal matter in Omaha with little notice, I booked a flight, hotel, and car rental. The miracle of points and miles is the ability to make anything happen when you really need it to without significant expense or inconvenience and I recommend to anyone that asks me about the loyalty space to leave a reserve to of 2.5x standard rates for an emergency trip home.

The flight was unremarkable (and priced about at that range, unfortunately), the hotel was a remodeled but otherwise unremarkable Hampton Inn, well located for my visit. But my typical rental car provider, National (owned by ERAC) was unavailable at the airport. I have some status with Avis and Hertz due to credit cards and reciprocal status but wanted to try the Drive Alliance angle for Enterprise companies. However, this required a nearby city location and not an airport rental. Honestly, it wasn’t that big of a deal to grab a Lyft to the downtown location at 23rd & Harney, and because of a credit, the ride only set me back $6.97 before tip.

Upon arrival, I was informed that my preferred car type was unavailable. For my trip a few vehicle types were offered, the cheapest being a mystery vehicle, but I opted for 2-4 levels above that for a Standard car and paid more for it. Not only was I told that the car I paid more for was not available, but that they only had minivans and there were zero other choices.

“Car choices aren’t guaranteed when booking within 24 hours.” There’s a little more context due, I know that car types are never guaranteed, but typically there’s more than just one type left.

“I don’t see that on my confirmation, can you show it to me?” She couldn’t, of course, then stated that “St. Louis”, ERAC headquarters, isn’t connected to their inventory. This opens a host of other questions. I searched the website, then I tried Google, then I enlisted AI and none of those options showed me specific adjustments described by the branch attendant stated by ERAC specific to the 24-hour booking period. I reached out to the brand on October 20th, it has yet to respond.

I had a choice to make, either take what they have or move on. As I was not at the airport and couldn’t just walk to another counter, I accepted my fate and moved to the garage.

The most unsavory part about the Enterprise experience as it differs from other brands is the endless damage evaluation. Walking around with an iPad, the attendant points out a knick here, a scratch there – the perfect moment to take out the insurance or pay with a card that includes the Collision Damage Waiver just to avoid participation.

I can’t say for certain that the vehicle was used to move pounds of marijuana across state lines – I couldn’t say that at all. But I could say for certain that it smelled so deeply of weed that I doubt any amount of cleaning could be effective.

“This one smells like weed.” I said, shutting the door.

“I’ll have to take your word for it.” She replied and moved on.

Really? Would you have noticed if I said it smelled as though a den of skunks had made their home in the stow-and-go or would you have to take my word for it? I don’t want to show up to family smelling like backstage at Coachella.

We moved on to the vehicle next to it, a California tag with 51,000 miles and a quarter tank of gas. She started the walk around again, noting that the chip in the windshield could spider but I wouldn’t be responsible if the windshield needed to be replaced upon my return. Cool. How about not giving me a vehicle where I might have a spiderwebbed safety issue?

I tossed my luggage inside, and addressed her one more time.

I had to address the fuel level, as I might not make it to my first stop without the low fuel light illuminating.

“A quarter tank?” I was borderline ready to leave but knew that I didn’t have time to start this all over somewhere else.

“Those two guys in the wash bay sitting down on their phones – do they work here?”

“Yes.” She said it to me unironically without connecting the challenge of the cleanliness, or the useless fuel level and how both of those service challenges might have been solved (in the case of the skunky van, maybe not) by the staff being asked to do their jobs.

They aren’t understaffed, they are unbothered, indifferent, and at a minimum unwilling to ask them to perform their duties, or more likely, incapable of actual management. It’s a crazy position to take with Enterprise’s excellent corporate structure and the fact that they give you the tools to be your own boss.

I guess some things are just better in the movies.

In the words of our 43rd US President, “Fool me once, shame on – shame on you. Fool me – you can’t get fooled again.” It was simpler times when that sort of turn of phrase failure was the height of presidential gaffes.

I don’t care that National’s ownership is the same (ERAC), I will continue to rent from them as long as their model remains the same and continues to deliver. But from Enterprise? Never, ever again. Maybe a “neighborhood location” has different rules, but the staff at the Downtown Omaha location exhibited a total lack of interest in my experience or their own jobs. Corporate didn’t respond to my survey nor to my request for comment. And while I would agree that I’m not Cooper Anderson reaching out to them, readers in the past have asked if the brand has a comment. They did not.

I shouldn’t have to drive around in a dented safety concern reeking of weed while I get gas immediately after departing the parking lot and somehow try to perfectly return with a quarter tank or pay $7/gallon. It’s disrespectful to your clients but it appears the great corporate structure at Enterprise may have given this branch the tools to be their own boss, and they were even less interested in doing that than I am in renting from any Enterprise location anywhere.

Besides renting from them in the first place, my greatest regret was that I didn’t get to try my credit card’s Collision Damage Waiver on for size, just in case I needed it.

Kyle is a freelance travel writer with contributions to Time, the Washington Post, MSNBC, Yahoo!, Reuters, Huffington Post, Travel Codex, PenAndPassports, Live And Lets Fly and many other media outlets. I have had terrible experiences with Enterprise in the past – being stranded with a disabled vehicle that could have been prevented by adequate maintenance, spurious cleaning charges, etc., I was forced to use Enterprise due to being at remote locations recently and was very pleased with their service. Sorry you were not as lucky.

I had a bad experience with Enterprise many years ago and stopped using them. A couple of years ago I booked with them when National was too expensive and had a good experience, and I have mostly booked with Enterprise ever since. All my recent experiences have been good. However, I have been booking almost exclusively at large or medium sized airports, so that could be the difference. They almost always have skip the counter and except at the largest airports they often share cars with National and Alamo anyway.

For best results, in an off airport location, try to use a car dealership. Perhaps one that has a relationship with friends or other local contacts. There you will find a few newer rentals in great condition that are not of skunk smell. These are not advertised but kept for the company. Cannot say they would honor t & c but at least you get a better choice.

You rented from Enterprise (at a non-airport) location. What could go wrong? Well, you learned what could go wrong.

From my experience, I’m not sure Enterprise is the problem. You wrote “maybe a neighborhood location has different rules” and I don’t think it’s different rules but perhaps different standards. And to be clear, this is the case for every rental car brand where I go to a neighborhood location – I used to do this often when I didn’t have a car, and I know that it is very different than the airport experience. Point by point… – Gas tank: more likely to be less than full, but that close to empty is particularly bad. In many neighborhood locations it is literally one person working the place. Still you need enough gas to drive it off the lot. – Cleanliness: Unacceptable. That sucks and reflects poorly on the brand. – Damage/Inspection: They always do the walkaround, and there’s almost always some damage they note. Many of mine had divots in the windshield or rear windshield and a couple door dings. Combined with there being one employee this process often means renting a car takes 20-30 minutes per person, which is another issue. – 24 hour rule: I don’t know of anywhere this is written but it is absolutely true at multiple brands that those booked within 24 hours are basically considered walk-ups in terms of availability. In fact there are usually printed signs when I go to the location saying as much. I rented from an Avis in a Portland suburb in the summer and multiple printed signs and a single unhappy employee greeted at least two people who had made reservations in the last day, showed up at 8am opening, and were turned away wholesale with no cars available on a random Thursday. I’m glad this story confirmed my assumption that it had to do with connection to real time inventory at corporate locations, as many neighborhood ones are franchises.

I do not disagree that this is a terrible experience, I’m just saying this is par for the course. I’ve rented at Enterprise, Hertz, and Avis neighborhood locations all with near-identical experiences, in San Diego, Portland, and San Francisco, for what it’s worth. Usually the neighborhood locations *inside* actual car dealerships (like a full-service Nissan dealer) are much better than the standalone or hotel-attached ones in the same city and have fewer of these problems, but they also tend to be open more limited hours.

Alex is right. Never use off-airport locations if you can avoid it. Most do not have good standards, and you are lucky if they have any decent car resembling the one you reserved available. If you have to, you might have slightly better luck at Hertz or Avis.

After some delays, United Airlines is one step closer to launching service on its posh new domestic plane.

The airline on Thursday evening announced it recently took delivery of its first Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” plane.

It’s a premium-heavy aircraft that will feature United’s new Polaris business-class suites and a true premium economy cabin.

And it will soon be a fixture on the carrier’s top transcontinental routes.

United shared a sneak peek of the new jet on social media Thursday evening —  well ... the outside of it, at least.

As expected, the exterior sports a special wrap featuring the “Coastliner” decal.

That’s because United plans to exclusively use this plane on its most premium coast-to-coast flights.

Once in service, you’ll see it on routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

It will likely also figure into the carrier’s plans at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), once United makes its long-awaited return to JFK.

While United had hoped to launch service on the Coastliner this past summer, delays at Airbus pushed the debut back a few months.

The jet is now slated to make its inaugural flight in early 2027, United said this week.

It will certainly be an upgrade to the airline’s prime transcontinental service.

Passengers flying in those suites will get access to United’s Polaris Lounge facilities.

There are also 12 Premium Plus recliners across three rows in a two-by-two configuration.

Plus, in economy there’s a walk-up snack bar.

The whole interior is very similar to the Airbus A321XLR that United debuted late this summer. That longer-range jet is slated to start flying to Europe in the coming months.

United’s looming introduction of the Coastliner comes as a growing number of U.S. carriers are upgrading their top transcontinental products.

This fall, Alaska Airlines revealed it will add lie-flat suites and premium economy to a future subfleet of Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets.

American Airlines last year launched coast-to-coast service with the A321XLR, which sports its latest-generation Flagship Suites up front.

Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, rolled out a version of the Airbus A321neo that doesn't have lie-flat seats (at least not yet) but does have a whopping 44 domestic first-class recliners.

Plus, JetBlue recently announced that passengers flying in its lie-flat Mint cabins would be entitled to enter its new airport lounges in New York City and Boston, even when flying domestically.

United has 50 of these Coastliners (along with 50 of the XLR jets) on order for the coming years.

So this aircraft will be a big part of the carrier’s most lucrative domestic service for years to come.

#6031. Where to Eat Gluten-Free in Montreal

Recently I’ve noticed more and more food people going to Montreal—and who can blame them? This laid-back bilingual gem on the St. Lawrence River is one of North America’s very best food cities. Personally I’ve loved it since my first visit almost 20 years ago. Montreal’s wonderful food scene draws me back year after year, sometimes multiple times,and by now the six-hour drive from my home in New York City feels like a breeze. It helps to know that my top meals of the year are waiting just across the border.

But for the past two years, following my wife’s celiac diagnosis, I have been navigating the city a little differently. When I was younger, trips to Montreal meant poutine, bagels, smoked-meat sandwiches, and a plethora of other canonical Québécois favorites that happen to be full of gluten. These days we prioritize other local favorites and have developed a dependable roster of businesses we trust—and that don’t feel like a compromise. Luckily there are a ton of them; we’ve been thrilled to discover that Montreal is a paradise for gluten-free eating.

In my opinion the only gluten-free Montreal-style bagels worth sampling are located in Burlington, Vermont. But Montreal is a city that takes its baked goods seriously, and it’s home to a handful of excellent dedicated gluten-free bakeries. You will not miss the bagels. Instead how about a croissant?

Any gluten-free eater knows croissants are one of the hardest pastries to get right without gluten. As a rule my wife and I don’t really bother—unless we’re in Montreal. At Boulangerie Le Marquis, near Jean-Talon Market, and sister business Le Marquis Signature Santé, in Old Montreal, magnificent pains au chocolat and gluten-free croissants—available in plain, almond, and chocolate-almond varieties—arrive hot out of the oven all morning long. Flaky laminated pastry is a near-impossible feat in the gluten-free world, but Le Marquis has perfected it. We favor the pains au chocolat and almond croissants, but it’s tough to go wrong.

Even more unique is the gluten-free manouché at La Bolo à Lolo, a GF market and takeaway in the Plateau. Chef and owner Gordy Moufarrej emigrated from Lebanon to Montreal as a boy and uses his mother’s homemade za’atar in these addictive flatbreads. Made from Moufarrej’s proprietary GF flour blend, they are topped with a paste of olive oil and za’atar, plus cheese if you want (you do). A number of sandwiches made with the same base are available, but we’ve never gotten past the manouché—on our last visit to Montreal, we went three days in a row.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a French-speaking city, crepes are another great option, and Montreal boasts an amazing spot for 100% buckwheat Breton-style galettes. At Crêperie du Marché, a bustling stall at Jean-Talon Market, cooks turn out a dedicated gluten-free menu of lacy galettes with both savory and sweet fillings. It’s a personal choice, but we like the cheeky selections that mix both: ham, cheese, eggs, potatoes, and a drizzle of maple syrup. Why not?

Nearby is cheery, quirky Cantine Panella, a dedicated gluten-free bakery and café run by the Peruvian chef Alessandra Perona. Her South American sensibility means breads are made with flours like quinoa, cassava, and sweet potato, which gives them a delightful chewiness. We like to stock up on a few of these to bring home, though they sometimes don’t last the drive.

Of all Montreal’s classic foods, rotisserie chicken might be my favorite. At Québécois-style rotisseries it’s slow-roasted on a spit and accompanied by gravy; at Portuguese spots it’s often spatchcocked and grilled over charcoal, then served with piri-piri sauce. In both cases gluten sometimes spoils the fun: Traditional establishments like the legendary Chalet Bar-B-Q and Portuguese eatery Ma Poule Mouillée both use wheat flour in their sauces. No matter—these are far from your only options.

Piri-Piri Chicken at Rôtisserie Coco Rico

At Rôtisserie Coco Rico, a Plateau institution open since 1970, the chicken is spit-roasted and served with GF piri-piri in a mélange of the two dominant local styles. On the side fries from a dedicated GF fryer are among the city’s best (and this is a city with great french fries), but don’t sleep on the roasted potatoes, full of savory chicken flavor.

More refined, and representing the French Canadian tradition, is Little Italy’s Rôtisserie La Lune, from the team behind überpopular restaurant and wine bar Mon Lapin. Gorgeous, plump birds are served with rich gluten-free gravy and excellent fries that come from a blessedly dedicated fryer. The same fryer is also responsible for the unbelievable Croqu’Ailes Farcies XL, which are deboned chicken wings stuffed with more chicken and deep-fried. Every meal here should start with these. But the kitchen has an equally deft hand with seasonal salads and veggie-focused sides—almost always gluten-free and an essential counterweight on the table.

Down the street from La Lune, Mon Lapin is equally adept at catering to gluten-free diners: On two recent visits most of the menu was in play. Dishes change with the seasons, but friendly servers will guide your choices (and help you navigate the impressive wine list). Make sure to save room for the restaurant’s signature buckwheat layer cake, accented with buckwheat honey caramel, fromage blanc, and crisp shards of buckwheat tuile. I’m not sure there’s a better gluten-free dessert on the continent.

Mon Lapin’s co-owners, chefs Jessica Noël and Marc-Olivier Frappier, and wine director Vanya Filipovic, are all alums of the trendsetting Little Burgundy eatery and wine bar Vin Papillon, whose chef and owner happens to be celiac. Best known as half of the duo that opened Montreal icon Joe Beef, Fred Morin now presides over those two restaurants, plus the rotisserie McKiernan and gastropub Liverpool House. His kitchens have airtight allergy protocols and are particularly sensitive to gluten-free diners because of Morin’s own celiac status. And because so many Montreal chefs have passed through Morin’s kitchens, his influence looms large over the city’s fine dining scene—and its spirit of hospitality toward those with allergies and intolerances.

While all of Morin’s restaurants are fantastic, Vin Papillon is the one we come back to every year—its Jambon de la Petite-Bourgogne is one of the world’s great meat-and-cheese plates, featuring house-cured ham, the Quebec sheep-milk cheese le Fleur des Monts, and a sneaky application of brown butter that brings together all the nutty, savory notes. For dessert the restaurant often serves a gluten-free carrot cake ice cream sandwich with caramel sauce in a silver goblet.

Another Joe Beef group alum, Ariel Schor, runs one of our favorite Verdun neighborhood spots with his brother, Pablo. Both natives of Argentina with Jewish roots, the Schors run a restaurant called Beba with a particular affinity for offal (organ meats) and a surprisingly light touch with creative veg dishes that change seasonally. Swiss chard leaves are stuffed with zucchini and chard stems and served with a sweet-and-sour condiment of onions, raisins, and pine nuts. Medjool dates are impishly filled with foie gras and topped with pistachio. Elsewhere on the menu expect things like tongue, rabbit, chorizo, and tripe—dishes that tend to be gluten-free.

When you’re craving Gallic comfort food, Montreal overdelivers. I used to think there were Leméac people and L’Express people, that one couldn’t possibly love Montreal’s two most prominent old-school bistros equally. I was wrong. The late local architect Luc Laporte designed both dining rooms, and they each have the buzzing, joyful energy most restaurants covet.

L’Express is my first love, a Montreal stalwart open since 1980 that I’ve been to more times than I can count. Its main virtues for gluten-free eaters are a dedicated fryer and incredibly good french fries—available as a stand-alone side or, even better, as part of steak frites. There are plenty of other GF mains and entrées, but room must be saved for the enormous île flottante, a classic French meringue-based dessert encased in a hardened caramel dome and surrounded by shards of candied almond. For something on the lighter side, try the unique crème brûlée with wild sweet clover from Quebec, sometimes called boreal vanilla.

Leméac does not have a dedicated fryer, so fries don’t work for celiacs. But I promise you won’t miss them. We favor the textbook duck confit, served with roasted potatoes and a bright green salad. For dessert there’s an unmissable gluten-free chocolate-and-banana moelleux, a decadent cake served with caramel and popcorn ice cream, along with many other classics, including crème caramel.

Montreal is also home to a number of fabulous Middle Eastern and North African restaurants, some of which can cater to gluten-free diners—albeit with asterisks. We love the standout Damas, a Syrian fine-dining spot on a pretty corner in Outremont, though gluten-free choices are limited. Still, it’s worth the trip for the ground lamb and eggplant kebab grilled over open charcoal and accompanied by charred pepper, tomato butter, and gobs of garlic labneh and the dreamy hummus topped with lamb shawarma and pine nuts, which can be served with crudités rather than pita. Both are among the best things I’ve eaten in recent memory.

Le Petit Alep, a neighborhood institution near Jean-Talon, offers more Syrian and Armenian options. The marvelous mezes are largely gluten-free and served—upon request—with crudités; savory, comforting mujaddara is made with lentils and rice, no bulgur, barley, or other glutenous grains. End with the house herbal tea, a beautiful floral mixture of cardamom pods, mint, rosewater, and orange blossom. I’ve tried to make it at home, but I can’t quite replicate it. That’s okay—I’ll be back next year.

#6030. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.

#6029. How to Watch the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade

As the turkey thaws and a day of cooking prep begins, an equally integral Thanksgiving tradition is Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Last year, 3.5 million spectators lined New York City’s streets to watch the procession of vibrant balloons and whimsical floats bob and weave through Midtown Manhattan to the beats of countless marching bands and celebrity performers. Beyond the city, a record-setting 34.3 million tuned into the NBC and Peacock broadcast, making the Emmy-winning production the year’s most-watched entertainment telecast. This year's promises to be even grander, as 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of the spectacle, which started in 1924 (though it wasn’t held from 1942 to 1944 because parade materials were reserved for wartime efforts).

“As a kid from the Bronx, it is an honor to bring this cherished tradition…to the city of New York every year,” the parade’s executive producer since 2021 Will Coss tells Condé Nast Traveler. The annual highlight for him is seeing the joyful expressions of spectators of all ages as the parade passes them by “showcasing some of the most iconic and recognizable pop culture characters and figures.”

This year marks the 99th anniversary of the Macy's Parade, an annual Thanksgiving tradition.

On the eve of the parade's centennial, the team—composed of painters, carpenters, animators, sculptures, welders, designers, engineers, and electricians—is honoring its past by way of revived classics like Felix the Cat and Underdog balloons. Ardent fans will also find a swath of newcomers that include a Fantasia-inspired Mickey, cowboy Minion, and a Peanuts duo. “The team at Macy’s Studios works year-round to make this historic parade bigger and better for our audiences every year,” Coss says. Here’s everything you need to know about the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026—all its surprises, delights, and familiar joys.

When Macy’s first debuted its one-million-square foot New York City flagship store at 34th Street between Broadway and Seventh Avenues in 1924, the retailer threw a Christmas parade on Thanksgiving morning to boost holiday sales—with a much longer route starting at 145 Street and Covent Avenue. Balloons joined the lineup in 1927, starting with Felix the Cat, and the festivities were first broadcast nationally in 1947.

These days, the festive parade follows a 2.5-mile path from the Upper East Side to Midtown Manhattan. Starting at the corner of 77th Street and Central Park West, the route heads south to Columbus Circle and then turns east, heading along 59th Street to Sixth Avenue. From there, it goes straight down Sixth Avenue to 34th Street, ending in front of Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square.

Clifford the Big Red Dog in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Coss recommends arriving early for a great view. Many spectators start to gather as early as 6 a.m. along the beginning of the route on Central Park West (approach from the west) from 61st to 75th Streets. Other prime spots include the south side of 59th Street between Columbus Circle and Sixth Avenue and the entire stretch of Sixth Avenue between 38th and 59th. Spectators should be aware there is no viewing on Central Park West between 59th and 60th Streets, or anywhere south of 38th Street.

Coss also reminds those bringing children to dress warmly for the chilly weather and to be prepared to entertain young ones for a few hours while waiting to spot the first float. He suggests avoiding strollers, large bags, backpacks, and umbrellas.

In celebration of its centennial, some 100 inflatables will fly. Returning after decades are much-anticipated Felix the Cat (the parade's first character balloon, introduced in 1927) and Blue Hippopotamus (from the 1931 parade), while Hello Kitty and Underdog (who appeared in every parade from 1965 through 1984) will also make cameos. New to the scene are Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, and Snoopy persona Joe Cool with Woodstock, among others. The procession will also welcome 52 floats, 31 clown crews, nine specialty units (such as trycaloons, or balloons ridden on tricycles), seven marching bands, and five balloonicles (that’s a balloon-vehicle hybrid).

TODAY’s Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker will host the live broadcast of the 100th Macy’s Parade. Though this year's performance lineup has yet to be announced, the 2025 roster featured 26 celebrity performers, ranging from Colbie Caillat and Christopher Jackson to Foreigner and Taylor Momsen, complete with a performance by KPop Demon Hunters’ HUNTR/X singing voices EJAE, Audrey Nuna, and Rei Ami. As anticipation for the parade's centennial only increases, Coss says this year will “bring new surprises and delights to the iconic holiday tradition and truly celebrate this incredibly special anniversary.”

For some, the majestic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an official marker of the transition into the Christmas season in New York City.

Americans can watch the live telecast on both NBC and Peacock on Thursday, November 26, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones, while Telemundo will air a Spanish-language simulcast hosted by Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz, and Clovis Nienow. For late risers, an encore will air starting at 2 p.m. ET/PT, and the full broadcast will also be on NBC with live audio description on Secondary Audio Program channel (SAP). Behind-the-scenes footage will be shared on social media @macys and #MacysParade via Instagram, TikTok, and Threads.

To rev up for the turkey day excitement, “Countdown to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade” will air on Wednesday, November 25, on NBC and Peacock. The primetime special will broadcast live from the parade starting line with exclusive previews and behind-the-scenes stories from the balloons and floats.

One of the most underrated—and free—ways to experience the parade is by attending the Thanksgiving Eve balloon inflating event on Wednesday, November 25, a “time-honored tradition and special peek into the parade celebrations,” Coss says. Since 1994, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has invited guests to see the process the balloons undergo to reach their larger-than-life size and scale the afternoon before Thanksgiving. Last year’s took place between 1 p.m. and 6 p.m., with the line opening at noon.

Those interested can enter at West 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, where they’ll be guided through a security checkpoint and then can roam between West 77th and 81st Streets to view the balloons. Note that prohibited items include bags or backpacks larger than 12-by-6-by-12 inches, lawn chairs, large coolers, alcoholic beverages, chairs, weapons, drones, pets, and umbrellas; participants will be screened before entering the route.

For the latest up-to-date information, visit macys.com/parade for details on the parade and nbc.com/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade for updates on the broadcast.

#6028. British Airways Boeing 787 Stranded In Pittsburgh For 2 Months Due To Complicated Repairs

A Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner has been stranded at Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) in Pennsylvania for over two months after reportedly sustaining significant damage during a ground-handling incident. The aircraft, registered as G-ZBJF, arrived at PIT from London Heathrow Airport (LHR) in August, operating as BA171. However, instead of a routine transatlantic arrival, a ground service vehicle collided with the aircraft, damaging its underside and leaving it unable to return to the skies.

More than 70 days later, the 12-year-old Dreamliner remains in Pittsburgh. According to Turbine Traveller, the repair process has proven to be much more complicated than initially anticipated. As several travelers reported, potential damage to the aircraft’s landing gear system continues to delay the repair process.

G-ZBJF arrived in Pittsburgh on August 28, after completing its roughly 3,233-nautical-mile (5,987 km) journey across the Atlantic Ocean. The aircraft departed Heathrow five minutes early, at 4:40 PM, and landed at PIT at approximately 8:23 PM local time. However, G-ZBJF never operated its return service to London later that night, and subsequent reports indicate the 787-8 sustained severe damage while on the ground. Flight tracking data and visual sightings confirm the aircraft is still on the ground.

According to discussions among aviation enthusiasts on Reddit, the incident that led to G-ZBJF’s grounding involved a mobile baggage belt loader that reportedly struck the airframe underneath one of its bulk cargo doors. The belt loader, a piece of ground service equipment used by ramp personnel to load and unload luggage from the 787’s cargo hold, was raised into position but pierced the fuselage, leaving a hole in the cargo bay’s exterior. Although the exact details beyond this have not been confirmed, the aircraft's continued presence in Pittsburgh suggests a major structural issue requiring a significant engineering solution.

The repair process could be particularly challenging given the 787’s construction. Unlike older aircraft that primarily use conventional aluminum structures, about 50% of the Dreamliner’s primary structure is made from composite materials. This includes significant portions of its fuselage and wings, requiring specialized inspection and repair procedures in the event of substantial structural damage.

Depending on the severity, British Airways maintenance engineers may have to construct a specialized patch to apply to the exterior of the Dreamliner. This would allow the plane to be ferried to a larger maintenance base capable of handling the 787, where more extensive work can be completed. In order to be transported to one of these locations, however, the aircraft would have to be approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to complete a one-off ferry flight via the use of a special flight permit (SFP).

Since the initial damage to G-ZBJF, several people have reported that the aircraft may also have damage to the landing gear system. According to one person on Reddit, a British Airways engineer who worked on the Dreamliner, repair work was well underway, but technicians encountered additional complications involving damage to the jet’s landing gear system. While this account has not been independently verified, it could help explain why the Dreamliner has remained grounded for so long.

A separate report suggests that British Airways could be preparing to reposition the airplane to Cincinnati Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG) after completing temporary repairs in Pittsburgh. The reported plan could allow the 787 to be moved to a larger facility operated by FEAM Aero, a maintenance services provider, where the aircraft could be repaired more permanently before returning to the United Kingdom. Ferrying the jet to Boeing’s 787 facilities in Seattle could also be another option, as the planemaker would be well-equipped to handle any repairs to the aircraft’s composite structure if needed.

For British Airways, getting G-ZBJF back into the skies is a high priority. Currently, the UK flag carrier operates a total of 12 examples of the 787-8, according to Planespotters.net. G-ZBJF is about 12 years old, first flying in April 2014 before being delivered to British Airways the following month. While it is not uncommon for airplanes to be parked for routine maintenance checks, the prolonged grounding of G-ZBJF is costing the airline not only potentially millions in repair fees, but hundreds of thousands in lost revenue potential and roughly $175,000 in gate parking charges, according to the Allegheny County Airport Authority (ACAA), which operates PIT. While British Airways likely is not paying the full amount given insurance coverage and the ground service operator's fault, it goes without a doubt that the airline would rather have its aircraft flying passengers than sitting on the ground in Pittsburgh.

The incident delayed the flight's departure by several hours.

Interestingly, the Pittsburgh incident is not the first time this year G-ZBJF has spent an extended period away from flying passengers. Before its latest grounding, the Dreamliner already spent nearly eight months at Cardiff Airport (CWL) in Wales, where British Airways operates a major maintenance facility, before being placed into long-term storage while D-checks were completed. Aircraft tracking records show that G-ZBJF arrived in Cardiff on December 19, 2025, and remained there until August 6. After nearly eight months in Cardiff, the aircraft returned to commercial operations on August 7, meaning it had been back in service for only about three weeks before being stranded in Pittsburgh.

G-ZBJF ferried to Cardiff for long-term storage and maintenance checks.

G-ZBJF completes D-check at Cardiff maintenance base.

G-ZBJF returns to operational service after being ferried from Cardiff to London.

G-ZBJF operates BA171 from LHR to PIT and is subsequently grounded in Pittsburgh after a ground service vehicle collided with the aircraft's underside.

The timing makes the latest incident particularly unfortunate for British Airways. Having spent much of the previous eight months undergoing extended maintenance, G-ZBJF had only recently returned to its regular flying schedule before the incident in Pittsburgh. Meanwhile, the prolonged grounding underscores the heavy logistical challenges of repairing a widebody thousands of miles from primary maintenance facilities. Whether the 787 can eventually return to service directly from Pittsburgh or must first be repositioned to another city remains one of the biggest unanswered questions.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I hope BA's insurers are going after the ground services provider for every farthing in damages.

Obviously its extended time in Cardiff at the BA maintenance base was due to its RR engines and the repair/upgrade of them. BA was smart to switch to GENex engines for its 787-10s.

I’ve held the (see rates and fees) for eight years, and despite carrying more than 25 credit cards, it’s one I’ll continue renewing year after year.

The reason is simple: World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and this card makes it even more rewarding to stay with the brand. Between an annual free night, automatic elite status and the ability to earn valuable Hyatt points on spending, I consistently receive far more value than the card’s affordable $95 annual fee.

It isn’t the right fit for everyone. Hyatt has a much smaller global footprint than Marriott, Hilton and IHG, so travelers who rarely stay at Hyatt hotels may be better served by a more flexible travel rewards card. However, if Hyatt is already part of your travel plans — or you’d like it to become one — the World of Hyatt card is one of the best mid-tier hotel cards on the market. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

If you’re comparing several hotel credit cards, here’s what you need to know at a glance:

Unlike cards that earn transferable rewards, this is very much a Hyatt-focused product. If you’re loyal to Hyatt — or want an affordable way to accelerate your progress toward higher status — it deserves serious consideration.

If there’s one reason why I continue paying the World of Hyatt card’s annual fee, it’s the anniversary free night certificate.

Each cardholder anniversary, you’ll receive a free night award valid at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort. Since Hyatt prices these properties between 3,000 and 25,000 points per night, there’s plenty of opportunity to extract well over $95 in value. Free nights expire 12 months after issuance.

I’ve redeemed my certificates at The Standard, Brussels, Hyatt House Manchester in the U.K. and Andaz Mexico City Condesa. In each case, paying cash would have cost considerably more than the card’s annual fee.

Even better, you can earn a second Category 1-4 certificate after spending $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

That’s the spending threshold I personally target each year. It unlocks another free night and an additional six elite night credits toward Hyatt status for even more value beyond the points you'll earn from that spending.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

Simply holding the card gives you complimentary Discoverist status.

While Discoverist isn’t Hyatt’s most rewarding elite tier, I still appreciate benefits like preferred room upgrades and late checkout (when available) and a 10% bonus on eligible Hyatt spending.

That said, for frequent Hyatt guests, this perk probably won’t be all that enticing since they’re likely to earn Discoverist status organically. The card becomes more valuable when working toward a higher status level.

Every calendar year, you’ll receive five qualifying night credits automatically, and you’ll earn another two qualifying night credits for every $5,000 spent.

I’ve found those elite night credits incredibly valuable. By combining the five annual elite nights from the card with my Hyatt stays and strategic spending to earn an additional six nights, I qualified for top-tier Globalist status in August 2025, which I’ll enjoy through February 2027.

Related: Was going all-in on Hyatt Globalist worth it? My honest take

Chase issues this card, so you'll receive several useful travel protections, including:

These protections aren't as extensive as those you'd receive with a premium travel card, but that's to be expected given this card's modest annual fee.

Related: Is the World of Hyatt credit card worth the annual fee?

One of my favorite things about the World of Hyatt program is that earning and redeeming points is refreshingly straightforward.

Unlike most major hotel loyalty programs, Hyatt still publishes an award chart, making award pricing more predictable.

When you stay at Hyatt hotels, these earnings stack with the points you earn as a World of Hyatt member. Since cardholders receive complimentary Discoverist status, you’ll also earn a 10% bonus on your base points, meaning you can earn up to 9.5 total points per dollar spent on eligible Hyatt purchases. That represents a solid 16% return on Hyatt purchases, per our November 2026 valuations.

I generally use this card for Hyatt stays and tax payments that help me reach the $15,000 annual threshold for the second free night certificate.

Otherwise, I typically use my  (see rates and fees) for most travel and dining purchases, then transfer those Chase Ultimate Rewards points to my Hyatt account whenever I need to top up my balance for an award stay.

That gives me the best of both worlds: I earn more rewards on everyday travel and dining while keeping my points flexible until I’m ready to book. If I don’t end up needing Hyatt points, I can always transfer them to one of Chase’s 13 other airline or hotel partners instead.

Related: 6 of the best credit cards for travel purchases — beyond flights and hotels

In my opinion, Hyatt points remain among the most valuable hotel points due to their flexibility.

Award nights start at just 3,000 points for a Category 1 property at the Lowest rate and range up to 75,000 points for a top-tier Category 8 property under Hyatt’s five-tier standard award chart.

I’ve used Hyatt points for everything from inexpensive city breaks to luxury resorts. Some of my favorite redemptions include:

Hyatt also lets you redeem points for Points + Cash stays, suite upgrades, club lounge access and Find experiences. While those options can make sense occasionally, I almost always get the best value by redeeming points for standard award nights.

Related: 22 best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

Despite being one of my favorite hotel credit cards, the won’t be the right fit for every traveler.

The biggest drawback is Hyatt’s relatively small footprint. While Hyatt has more than 1,500 hotels and all-inclusive properties across 80-plus countries, that’s still far fewer than Marriott or Hilton. If you frequently travel to destinations without a Hyatt, you may struggle to maximize the card’s benefits.

Those who prioritize earning the highest possible rewards on everyday spending will likely find better options elsewhere. Beyond Hyatt purchases and spending toward the $15,000 threshold for a second free night certificate, this card isn’t particularly rewarding for dining, travel or everyday purchases.

Finally, travelers looking for premium perks like airport lounge access, annual travel credits and luxury benefits across multiple hotel brands should consider a premium travel rewards card instead.

For most travelers, I think the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card is the better choice than the (see rates and fees).

Both cards help you earn Hyatt points and elite status, but the business version is designed primarily for business owners. It offers bonus categories geared toward business spending and additional benefits for companies, while the personal card provides better long-term value for most travelers, thanks to its annual Category 1-4 free night certificate.

By comparison, I think the World of Hyatt Business card's $199 annual fee is harder to justify year after year because it lacks an anniversary free night. It does offer up to $100 in Hyatt statement credits each anniversary year, but that requires Hyatt spending and there's no way to get outsized value like you might with a free night.

Unless you own a business and can maximize the business-specific earning categories, I’d start with the personal card.

Related: World of Hyatt card vs. World of Hyatt Business card: 2 valuable hotel earners

The currently offers new cardholders four free nights (at Category 1-4 Hyatt hotels) after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

These are hotels that would ordinarily require 3,000 to 25,000 points per night, depending on the property and stay dates. Someone who uses all four free night certificates at the highest-priced properties would save up to 100,000 World of Hyatt points, making this offer worth up to $1,650 (based on TPG valuations).

This is a very strong bonus compared to other historical welcome offers, though not the absolute all-time highest offer for new cardmembers. The best-ever welcome offer included five free-night awards (offer no longer available). Having said that, if you max out the four certificates, this would be considered the most lucrative offer since February.

Despite being a great offer right now, some travelers may prefer to wait until the introductory bonus is awarded in points instead. Unlike free nights, there are no hotel category restrictions for redeeming points. The expiration date for free nights is also stricter.

If you’d rather earn more flexible rewards that are transferable to a number of travel partners, including Hyatt, one of these cards may be a better fit:

I’ve carried the World of Hyatt Credit Card for eight years, and it’s one of the few hotel credit cards I have no intention of canceling.

The annual Category 1-4 free night certificate has consistently offset the card’s $95 annual fee, while the elite night credits helped me qualify for Globalist status last year. Add in Hyatt’s strong redemption value, and it’s easy to see why this remains my favorite mid-tier hotel credit card.

If you regularly stay at Hyatt properties, I think the World of Hyatt card deserves a place in your wallet. If you rarely stay with Hyatt, though, you’ll probably get more long-term value from a flexible travel rewards card.
